Correlates in Female Athletes: Differences
in Team and Individual Sports
Authors: Haase, A.M.
Population subgroup:
84 Team sport types
53 Individual sport types
Inclusion criteria: Fema athletes competing in team sports and individuals sports; athletes were competing at national and international competitions
Mean_Age:
Team sport M=19.71, SD=3.82
Individual sport M=19.16, SD=3.49
Soccer M=19.00, SD=4.25
Netball M=20.17, SD=2.87
Volleyball M=21.08, SD=4.06
Aerobics M=18.70, SD=3.18
Diving M=19.90, SD=3.91
Mean_BMI:
Team sport type M=21.69, SD=1.99
Individual sport type M=21.02, SD=1.92
Soccer M=21.46, SD=1.86
Netball M=22.03, SD=2.06
Volleyball M=21.59, SD=2.22
Aerobics M=21.16, SD=1.87
Diving M=20.83, SD=2.02
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Authors' conclusions: SPA scores contributed to dieting and bulimia scores in individual athletes. SPA and sport type independently and in combination contribute to greater dieting and bulimic behavior, particularly in Female individual sport athletes.
Limits: Only athletes attending the training would have been approached about the study. Not all athletes from each sport at each institute were present at the time of data collection due to other commutmalets. Most athletes were tested at training sessions, rather than in settings which might heighten SPA. The testing of athletes in this manner may identify more consistent levels of SPA and disordered eating. This division by team and individual sport may be too simplisticc, not accounting for other psychological and confounding factors. These factors may affect disordered eating.
Perspectives:
Longitudinal and experimental designs may elucidate the directionality of the relationship, providing support for possible interventions. 
Female indivdiual sport athletes in particular may benefit from practical methods of reducing SPA and encouraging healthy eating within the sport setting by coaches and peers. 
Attention to other trigger factors may be necessary when dealing with Female athletes in individual sports, as this subgroup reported the highest levels of dieting and bulimic tendencies, along with high SPA. Different techniques and strategies for dealing with SPA and disordered eating may be required for different sport types.
Sport_name_original: Netball; soccer; volleyball; aerobics; diving

Title: Individual differences in male body image: an examination of self-objectivation in recreational body builders
Authors: Hallsworth, L., Wade, T., Tiggemann, M.
Inclusion criteria: Males. The first group consisted of bodybuilders; minimum level of training twice a week for at least a year. The second group consisted of competitive weightlifters recruited from the state weightlifting associations in four states of Australia.
Mean_Age:
Bodybuilders M=28.89, SD=6.19
Weightlifters M=27.60, SD=8.70
Non-athletic control M=26.43, SD=8.15
Mean_BMI:
Weightlifters M=28.60, SD=6.90
Bodybuilders M=26.04, SD=3.08
Controls M=24.18, SD=2.80
Mean_Exercise frequency:
Bodybuilders M=6.40 hours per week
Weightlifters M=12.12 hours per week 
Controls M=3.8 hours per week
Mean_Years of experience:
Bodybuilders M=6.14 years
Weightlifters M=9.06 years
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Authors' conclusions: Bodybuilding may represent a practice that encourages male to become more self-conscious of their bodies, putting them at greater risk of experiencing greater levels of monitoring of body appearance and anxiety about physical appearance. This body self consciousness is associated with a greater risk of body dissatisfaction and drive for muscularity. Weightlifting does not appear to represent an objectifying climate.
Limits: The cross sectional nature makes it possible only to speculate on the directions of causality. Unequal sample sizes of groups in our analyses, particularly with respect to fewer competitive weightlifters. Unknown selection bias that may be operating in the bodybuilder and weightlifter groups, and any subsequent influence on the interpretation of our results. The weighlifting and bodybuilder groups differed not only in the nature of their sport, but also in competitive nature of this sport, which may introduce confound for differences found between the groups.
Perspectives: Health pursuits for male should emphasize achievement and function rather than appearance if they are to avoid deleterious consesquences.
Sport_name_original: Bodybuilding, Weightlifting, Soccer, football, running, martial arts, swimming

Title: How the obsession to eat healthy food meets with the willingness to do sports: the motivational background of orthorexia nervosa
Authors: Kiss-Leizer, M., Toth-Jiraly, I., & Rigo, A.
Inclusion criteria: Participants aged between 18 to 72 years
Range_Exercise frequency:
37.2% 3-4 times per week
25.8% 1-2h weekly
25% 3-4h 
35.2% for 5 or more than 5h
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Authors' conclusions: Health anxiety, mood modification are a strong predictor of orthorexia nervosa.
Limits: The results of the present study were based on online data gathering which questions the representative nature of the sample. Although participants were represented in a broad range of age and educational level, the highest proportion of participants were young and highly qualified Female. The participation in the research was voluntary thus the increased interest towards the topic of the examination might bias the results. The correlational desing of the present study does not allow causal inferences. The subject of the present study was the tendency to orthorexia nercosa, not orthorexia nervosa as a diagnosis, the results cannot be fully transposed into orthorexia nervosa since no orthorexia diagnosed patients are available yet.
Perspectives: A viable next step in orthorexia nervosa research could be the use of experience sampling method which could provide important information about the daily fluctuation of orthorexia nervosa and the related variables. It would be benefical to collect information about the type of the exercise as well, because some sport activities (category sports, aesthetic sport) can mean a higher vulnerability to orthorexia.

Title: Social physique anxiety and disturbed eating attitudes and behaviors in adolescents: moderating effects of sport, sport related characteristics, and gender
Authors: Lanfranchi, M.C., Maiano, C., Morin, A.J.S., & Therme, P.
Population subgroup:
Not involved in sport practice (n=431)
Involved in sport practice (n=335)
Inclusion criteria: Adolescents aged between 11 and 18 years.
Sport_name: 46 different sports categorized on (1) leanness, (2) nonleanness, (3) individual, (4) team, (5) organized or (6) not, (7) competitive or (8) not
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Authors' conclusions: The results demonstrating a significant and positive relationship between social physique anxiety and Disordered eating (i.e., generic Disordered eating, vomiting-purging behaviors, eating related control). Higher levels of SPA tend to be more associated with high levels of eating related control for boys and girls, this relation is more pronounced for boys.
Limits: Cross-sectional design, precluding examination of the directionality of the associations between SPA and Disordered eating. This study focused on the use of Disordered eating as a coping strategy for physical self-presentational concerns related to thinness or leanness. The fact that this study fails to consider concerns specifically related to muscularity and their possible relation with Disordered eating is an important limitation. No distinction was made for sports where the main emphasis is on muscularity, weight gain, or even drastric weight control (e.g., body building, football, power lifting). Less than half of the adolescents were involved in competitive sports and most did so at a nonelite level. We cannot identify the moderating role of the type of competition on the relationship between SPA and Disordered eating. This study neglected to examine more pathogenic behaviors (i.e., fasting, use of laxatives and/or diuretics, enemas, appetite suppressants) that adolescents could use to their physique. We do not know whether SPA is associated with the pathogenic weight control behaviors that adolescents engage in or whether sport practice is a moderator of this relationship.
Perspectives:
Consideration of the potential impact on muscularity oriented and weight control sports in the relationships between SPA, gender and Disordered eating should be the object of future studies. 
Culture is known to play an important role in the definition of body shape ideals and thus may exert a significant impact on the relationships observed in the current study. 
To further extend the current results, it would be interesting for future research to focus more specifically on the role of (a) body related sport motives (i.e., weight and shape control, weight loss, improvement of ones appearance), (b) social comparison processes and/or social physique pressure, and (c) socio contextual factors (parents, peers, coaches) of sport practices in the relationships between SPA, gender, sport practice and Disordered eating. 
One strategy that clinicians could adopt to prevent or reduce the development of high levels of Disordered eating in adolescents would be to focus on the reduction of high levels of physical self-presentation concerns ; adopt healthy coping strategies for dealing with SPA levels.

Title: Does coping mediate the relationship between competitive anxiety and eating disorders in athletes ?
Authors: De Sousa Fortes, L., do Nascimaleto Junior, J.R.A., Freire, G.L.M., & Ferreira, M.E.C.
Inclusion criteria: Minimum training of eight hours per week; minimum participation in a competition of regional dimension in 2016; be available to answer questionnaires and participate in anthropometric evaluations. The criteria for athletes exclusion were: 1. to present physical or intellectual disability; 2. to have taken psychoactive medications in the six months prior ro the research.
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Authors' conclusions: The structural equation model has pointed out a direct relationship between competitive anxiety and eating disorder. These findings indicated that stress perception during competitive events and negative thoughts about competitive performance were associated with the triggering of eating disorders in Brazilian male athletes.
Limits: Since we used self-reported instruments as assessment tools, the result may not reflect th context analyzed, because the responses were subjective. Portuguese is the langage spoken in Brazil and Portugal, but these countries have significant cultural differences and also small changes in their own writing. In this sense, the use of such a psychometric instrument in this study may have influenced the results obtained. Another limitation is that we used only the total score of the instruments, maling impossible the mediating role of ACSI-28 subscales in the association between anxiety and eating disorders. In addition, this study was restricted to the evaluation of psychological variables of athletes in just one moment, which does not characterize the real relationships of cause and effect between the variables.
Perspectives:
Future investigations should use a prospective approach with the athletes, besides crossing the previously described psychological variables with the performance levels during the season. 
We suggest further investigations with male Brazilian athletes to confirm the findings of this study. Furthermore, it is recommaleded the construction of an etiological model of eating disorder for Brazilian athletes of both sexes. The practical results of this study are in the possibility of sports professionals, more specifically, sports psychologists, to develop interventions that make it possible to decrease the level of competitive anxiety and/or enhance the development of coping strategies to reduce the triggering of eating disorders in Brazilian male athletes.

Title: mental skills as protective attributes against eating disorder risk in dancers
Authors: Estanol, E.
Inclusion criteria: The majority of participants were European American collegiate ballet dancers; however, collegiate modern and professional ballet dancers were also included in the sample. In order to ascertain a sample more less representative o the US population, the companies and universities were selected based on geographic location (east coast, midwest and western states). Selection of universities was also made by locating programs that had pre-professional or elite dance programs.
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Authors' conclusions: Negative affect (depression and anxiety), and weight pressures in the dance environment were positively associated with ED symptoms. mental skills were found to be negatively asscoiated with ED symptoms. Negative affect partially mediated the relationship between weight pressures and ED symptoms. mental skills, specifically coping with adversity, freedom from worry, and confidence/achievement motivation, fully mediated the relationship between negative affect and ED symptoms. Total score for the athletic coping skill inventory was signficantly negatively correlated with weight pressure in dance, anxiety, depression and eating disorder risk.
Limits: One limitation of this study was that the sample was predominantly white and Female. Results from this study may therefore not be generalizable to a more ethnically diverse sample or to male dancers. Furthermore, this study lacked a comparison group of non-dancers, which would have enabled the researchers to more objectively compare the impact of the dance environment with a non-dance environment.
Perspectives: Additional studies are needed to explore how other protective factors (i.e., satisfaction with life, optimism, self-esteem, humor, and spirituality) may further explain variations in ED symptoms in dancers and contribute to this mediation model identified. Future research that looks at variables in the context of high-risk groups by providing profiles of resilient dancers vs at-risk dancers is also needed in order to further clarify the relationship between risk and resilience factors and ED outcomes. Furthermore, including demographic variables in the analyses would help us to better understand if certain subpopulations of dancers, may be more at risk or protected from pressures in the dance environment. Finally, studies should include the use of alternative methods in addition to self-report to more thoroughly explore variables relating to the dance environment.

Title: Disordered eating attitudes, anxiety, self esteem and perfectionism in young athletes and non athletes
Authors: Petisco-Rodriguez, C., Sanchez-Sanchez, L.C., Fernandez-Garcia, R., Sanchez-Sanchez, J., & Garcia-Montes, J.M.
Journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
Population subgroup:
40 Athletes competing in rhythmic gymnastics
40 Athletes competing in football
40 Non-athletes
Inclusion criteria: Membership in Spanish sport clubs or rhythmic gymnastics, or footballers with a background > 4 years of systematic training and competitive experience, training a minimum of 8h per week, with absence of severe injuries
Mean_Age:
Gymnasts M=16.6, SD=2.62
Footballers M=17.98, SD=3.42
Mean_BMI:
M=20.63, SD=2.77
Gymnasts M=18.72, SD=1.54
Footballers M=22.45, SD=2.93
Sporting population: Gymnasts group consisted of 5 elite competing internationally and 35 at the national level
Range_Exercise frequency:
Elites : 20-35h per week
National gymnasts : 12-20h per week
Footballers : 4 training sessions plus a competitive match per week
Range_Years of experience: Minimum 4 years of training and competitive experience
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Authors' conclusions: Correlation obtained between anxiety (both trait and state) and the EAT-40 was positively and statistically significant. In the multiple regression analysis that was performed with SCOFF scores as a dependent variable, the most predictive variable was socially prescribed perfectionism. It showed negative correlation with EAT-40 and self esteem. Self esteem is probably a protective factor to develop an eating disorder despite perfectionism, which is the most predictive variable as the multiple linear regression showed, and this variable was high in athletes.
Limits: Small sample size. No precise clinical diagnostic data were available to validate ED screening in the current study.
Perspectives:
In the future, the use of other kinds of measurements, less subjected to the desirability bias, would help to discriminate whether the improvements in self-esteem and eating disorders in elite gymnasts are due to this bias or to preventing psychological treatments and trainings by coaches.
 In addition, it is important to further explore the impact of other psychological factors on eating disordered behaviours such as body image, mood, depression or motivation, among others; due to the fact that they imply multifactorial aetiology of disorders.

Title: Psychosocial correlates of disordered eating among male collegiate athletes
Authors: Petrie, T.A., Greenleaf, C., Carter, J.E., & Reel, J.J.
Population subgroup:
Asymptomatic group based on their QEDD responses (n=164)
Symptomatic group based on their QEDD responses (n=35)
Inclusion criteria: Male collegiate athletes from three different NCAA division I institutions located in the Midwest, Southwest and Mountain regions of the US
Mean_Years of experience:
College level M=1.81, SD=1.30
M=8.70, SD=5.28
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Authors' conclusions: The psychosocial factors generally were unrelated to level of eating pathology. The male athletes were healthy in terms of their eating behaviors, had few negative mood concerns, were moderately satisfied with their bodies and experienced few pressures from personal and societal sources to change their weight or body size/shape.
Limits: Negative mood was represented by a single-item measures, this may have affected the relationship with disordered eating. All data are based on athlete self report and thus are subject to mono-method bias as well as underreporting that might occur when assessing sensitive areas. Only two of the male athletes were classified as having an eating disorder and both had an ED-NOS.
Perspectives: Researchers should use measures of specific mood states (e.g., depression, anxiety) that are based on multiple items (e.g., PANAS-X), include measures of positive mood state (e.g., optimism, happiness, confidence) and incorporate designs (e.g., longitudinal) that allow these questions to be addressed directly. Professionals should be attuned to looking for subclinical level presentations of symptoms among the athletes with whom they work. Professionals may want to work proactively with male athletic teams, educating them about healthy, nutritional eating and maintaing regular exercise during the off-season. Such approaches may assist male collegiate athletes during the shift from the structural regimen that occurs when in-season and the potentially more relaxed, self-initiated approach that is taken during the off season.

Title: Emotion dysregulation mediates the relationship between psychological distress, symptoms of exercise addiction and eating disorders: a large-scale survey among fitness centers users
Authors: Kun, B., Urban, R., Szabo, A., Magi, A., Eisinger, A., & Demetrovics, Z.
Inclusion criteria: Members of various urban fitness centers aged between 18 and 60 years
Mean_Exercise frequency:
General week almost five sessions M=4.84, SD=2.80
General week was almost 7hr M=6.73, SD=4.36
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Authors' conclusions: Emotion dysregulation is an expected possible risk factor for both exercise addiction and eating disorders. The difficulties in emotion regulation strongly meduated the relationship between psychological symptoms and eating disorders in Female and explained 52.7% of the total indirect effect compared to the much lower 17.3% in male.
Limits: We adopted a cross sectional design and we conducted statistical mediation analyses. Although mediation might assume any casual relationships, our design and data are not suitable for confirming any cause and effect relationships. Furthermore, our model is based solely on theoretical assumptions and the current design cannot help to refute neither the alternative not the possible equivalent models. The nature of self rating instruments implies several possible biases (social desirability, insufficient self knowledge, distorsion of the memory processes) we should consider in interprating the results. Using self report questionnaire by collecting data at the same time from the same individuals raises the bias of common method variance. We used screening methods for assessing both eating disorders and exercise addiction, and these instruments are not applicable for making diagnoses. The SCOFF questionnaire showed a questionable internal consistency in the present sample. We examined a wide range of regular exercisers which may down tune the exposed results, since in a group of high-volume exercisers the current findings may possibly be amplified.
Perspectives: This study should be replicated with avid exercisers training for at least 10hr or more per week.

Title: The relationship between exercise addiction, eating disorders, and insecure attachment styles among recreational exercisers

Title: Application of the transdiagnostic cognitive-behavioral model of eating disorders to the athletic population
Authors: Shanmugam, V., Jowett, S., & Meyer, C.
Inclusion criteria: Males and Females British athletes
Sporting population: 31% elite athletes competing at the international or national level, 69% non elite competing for county/regional, 20% club and 30% university teams
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Authors' conclusions: Avoidant attachmalet was associated with poor quality relationships with their influential parent and principal coach. Athletes who experiencd more conflict in their relationships were more likely to criticize themselves, which in turn can be related to low self esteem, with athletes feeling unvalued and worthless as indivdiuals. Subsequently, low self esteem was linked to higher depressive symptoms, which in turn was lined to eating psychopathology. Self critical perfectionism may play a more pivotal role in eating psychopathology than personal standard perfectionism. The possession of high self imposed standards may not be related to eating psychopathology. The psychopathological process of perfectionism and self esteem both seem to exert an indirect effect on eating psychopathology, while depression exerts a direct effect.
Limits: The study was cross sectional. There are some limitations related to the operational definitions and measurement of the constructs related to the transdiagnostic cognitive behavioral model. In this study only one aspect of the concept of mood intolerance was captured. The current study employed self report measures, results are subject to social desirability and acquiescence response bias. The study did not use a control group of non athletes and a sample of athletes with eating disorders. It therefore remains unclear whether the relationships observed would extend to the nonathletic population or to clinical populations.
Perspectives: Continuing to develop a more encompassing understanding of the risk factors associated with eating disorders in athletes (e.g., examining psycho-social risk factors in addition to the sport-specific risk factors) wa may come a step closer in being able to prevent, manage and treat the disorder within the broader sporting community.

Title: Interpersonal difficulties as a risk factor for athletes eating psychopathology
Authors: Shanmugam, V., Jowett, S., & Meyer, C.
Journal: Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports
Inclusion criteria: British athletes
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Authors' conclusions: Negative and positive aspects of the quality of the coach athlete and teammate athlete were related to athletes eating psychopathology after controlling for baseline eating psychopathology score. Conflict with the coach was found to be the only significant independent predictor of athletes eating psychopathology. The quality of the relationship with parents and attachmalet styles were not found to be related to athletes eating psychopathology 6 months later.
Limits: The present findings are essentially correlational, thus preventing definitive conclusions about causality. The present study only examined the direct role of interpersonal relationships in atletes eating psychopathology. Fairburn et al. (2003) noted that interpersonal difficulties interact with other core psychopathological processes (low self esteem, clinical perfectionism, and mood intolerance) to potentially elicit and maintain eating disorders.
Perspectives: Future studies should seek to examine how such processes as clinical perfectionism, self esteem, and mood intolerance interact with interpersonal difficulties to elicit eating psychopathology . And investigaite how these interpersonal variables interact with each other to predict athletes eating psychopathology.

Title: Disordered eating attitudes, anxiety, self esteem and perfectionism in young athletes and non athletes
Authors: Petisco-Rodriguez, C., Sanchez-Sanchez, L.C., Fernandez-Garcia, R., Sanchez-Sanchez, J., & Garcia-Montes, J.M.
Journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
Population subgroup:
40 Athletes competing in rhythmic gymnastics
40 Athletes competing in football
40 Non-athletes
Inclusion criteria: Membership in Spanish sport clubs or rhythmic gymnastics, or footballers with a background > 4 years of systematic training and competitive experience, training a minimum of 8h per week, with absence of severe injuries
Mean_Age:
Gymnasts M=16.6, SD=2.62
Footballers M=17.98, SD=3.42
Mean_BMI:
M=20.63, SD=2.77
Gymnasts M=18.72, SD=1.54
Footballers M=22.45, SD=2.93
Sporting population: Gymnasts group consisted of 5 elite competing internationally and 35 at the national level
Range_Exercise frequency:
Elites : 20-35h per week
National gymnasts : 12-20h per week
Footballers : 4 training sessions plus a competitive match per week
Range_Years of experience: Minimum 4 years of training and competitive experience
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Authors' conclusions: Correlation obtained between anxiety (both trait and state) and the EAT-40 was positively and statistically significant. In the multiple regression analysis that was performed with SCOFF scores as a dependent variable, the most predictive variable was socially prescribed perfectionism. It showed negative correlation with EAT-40 and self esteem. Self esteem is probably a protective factor to develop an eating disorder despite perfectionism, which is the most predictive variable as the multiple linear regression showed, and this variable was high in athletes.
Limits: Small sample size. No precise clinical diagnostic data were available to validate ED screening in the current study.
Perspectives:
In the future, the use of other kinds of measurements, less subjected to the desirability bias, would help to discriminate whether the improvements in self-esteem and eating disorders in elite gymnasts are due to this bias or to preventing psychological treatments and trainings by coaches.
 In addition, it is important to further explore the impact of other psychological factors on eating disordered behaviours such as body image, mood, depression or motivation, among others; due to the fact that they imply multifactorial aetiology of disorders.

College level M=1.71, SD=1.27
M=8.89, SD=4.80
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Authors' conclusions: The pressures participants felt from general media (e.g., magazines, television/movies) rather than from sport-specific (e.g., teammates, judges) and interpersonal (e.g., boy/girlfriend, friends) sources most strongly discriminated among the three eating disorder categories. The correlations between internalization and the discriminant functin were significant but small. Athlete, relative to nonathletes, may be more satisfied with their bodies, this variable is related strongly to eating pathology. Body image, internalization, negative affect and pressures contributed similarly to the differentiation among the three eating disorder categories.

Future sudies may want to employ Petrie and Greenleaf's (2007) conceptual model using structural equation modeling and incorporate qualitative interviews to better determine how Female athletes experience and cope with the pressure from coaches, and whether these pressures change over the time they are involved in their sports. Professionals need to develop methods for screening athletes prior to each season to identify eating disorder and symptomatic groups and intervene as early as possible. Body image groups that focus on decreasing internalization and the effects of societal pressures may be an effective intervention strategy with Female athletes.

Title: The relationship between perceived stress, body image and eating behaviors in athletes
Authors: Şentürk, G., Deliceoğlu, G., Atasoy, M., & Yıldırım, İ.G.
Journal: Research in Sport Education and Sciences
Inclusion criteria: Athletes between the ages of 13-23 who volunteered to participate
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Authors' conclusions: Perfectionism in athletes is linked to higher stress, eating disturbances, and body perception issues, with women showing higher stress, emotional eating, and restrictive eating behaviors. Emotional states significantly influence eating patterns, highlighting the need for psychological and nutritional support in sports contexts
Limits: Findings are partly inconsistent with previous studies (e.g., gender differences), and results may depend on specific sports or samples. The study also relies on self-reported measures, which may introduce bias
Perspectives: Future research should further explore emotional eating across different sports and genders, and develop targeted interventions. Integrating psychological support, education, and nutritional guidance could help improve athletes’ well-being and performance

Title: Bulimic symptomatology among male collegiate athletes: a test of an etiological model
Authors: Chatterton, J., Petrie, T.A., Schuler, K.L., & Ruggero, C.
Inclusion criteria: Male collegiate athletes drawn from 35 states in the United States; athletes competed at the National Collegiate Athletic Association Division I, II, III and National Association of Intercollegiate Athletes levels.
Sporting population: National Collegiate Athletic Association Division I, II, III and National Association of Intercollegiate Athletes levels
Related_Factor_measure: Scale for muscle building behaviors and muscularity oriented body image subscales
Related_Factor_CLASS: Unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Authors' conclusions: Sport specific pressures played the most important role in understanding the athletes symptomatology, having effects through negative affect, dietary restraint and drive for muscularity. As the direct precursors of the athletes bulimic symptomatology, body dissatisfaction, negative affect, dietary restraint and drive for muscularity were also salient.
Limits: First due to lack of fit, we defined drive for muscularity solely by the muscularity behaviors items. Second the current study used a cross-sectional design that did not allow for a causal, or temporal, interpretation of the data. Third, although the current study used a large sample of male collegiate athletes in the United States, athletes self-selected into the study and certain sport were underrepresented. Therefore, the findings may not generalize to all sports. Finally, our measure of general societal appearance ideals was broad and did not include specific references to the body, weight and appearance pressures indivdiuals might experience through their involvmalet in social media.
Perspectives: In future studies, researchers might examine the supported relationships longitudinally, such as between sport weight pressures and dietary restraint or drive for muscularity, to determine how they change over time and which variables temporally influence others. Future research might test this model within single sports (e.g., all football players or all soccer players) or among younger athletes to determine if the influence of the sport environment remains, is heightened, or is diminished. Programs designed to educate coaches about the impact of their remarks and that highlight self-awareness regarding such comments could be implemented to help shift the focus of the athletic environment away from weight and appearance. Sport psychologist also might work directly with athletes, providing them with resources and strategies for countering the ubiquitous messages about physical and appearance ideals. Furthermore, athletic departments might develop annual screening for their athletes that could carried out by sports medicine personnel such as athletic trainers. This screening could be done to identify athletes who report high levels of body dissatisfaction, a high drive to restrict their eating and a strong focus on muscle building behaviors.

Inclusion criteria: Male collegiate athletes drawn from 35 states in the United States; athletes competed at the National Collegiate Athletic Association Division I, II, III and National Association of Intercollegiate Athletes levels.
Sporting population: National Collegiate Athletic Association Division I, II, III and National Association of Intercollegiate Athletes levels
Related_Factor_measure: Scale for muscle building behaviors and muscularity oriented body image subscales
Related_Factor_CLASS: Unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Authors' conclusions: Sport specific pressures played the most important role in understanding the athletes symptomatology, having effects through negative affect, dietary restraint and drive for muscularity. As the direct precursors of the athletes bulimic symptomatology, body dissatisfaction, negative affect, dietary restraint and drive for muscularity were also salient.
Limits: First due to lack of fit, we defined drive for muscularity solely by the muscularity behaviors items. Second the current study used a cross-sectional design that did not allow for a causal, or temporal, interpretation of the data. Third, although the current study used a large sample of male collegiate athletes in the United States, athletes self-selected into the study and certain sport were underrepresented. Therefore, the findings may not generalize to all sports. Finally, our measure of general societal appearance ideals was broad and did not include specific references to the body, weight and appearance pressures indivdiuals might experience through their involvmalet in social media.
Perspectives: In future studies, researchers might examine the supported relationships longitudinally, such as between sport weight pressures and dietary restraint or drive for muscularity, to determine how they change over time and which variables temporally influence others. Future research might test this model within single sports (e.g., all football players or all soccer players) or among younger athletes to determine if the influence of the sport environment remains, is heightened, or is diminished. Programs designed to educate coaches about the impact of their remarks and that highlight self-awareness regarding such comments could be implemented to help shift the focus of the athletic environment away from weight and appearance. Sport psychologist also might work directly with athletes, providing them with resources and strategies for countering the ubiquitous messages about physical and appearance ideals. Furthermore, athletic departments might develop annual screening for their athletes that could carried out by sports medicine personnel such as athletic trainers. This screening could be done to identify athletes who report high levels of body dissatisfaction, a high drive to restrict their eating and a strong focus on muscle building behaviors.
Sport_name_original: Baseball, football, track and field, swimming/diving, soccer, basketball, cross-country, tennis, wrestling, lacrosse, golf, ice hockey, crew, fencing, volleyball, skiing and squash

Title: Perfectionism and eating attitudes in competitive rowers: moderating effects of body mass, weight classification and gender
Authors: Haase, A.M., Prapavessis, H., & Owens, G.
Inclusion criteria: National level heavyweight and lightweight rowers from New Zealand and Australia
Mean_Age:
Female M=20.08, SD=4.23
Male M=21.49, SD=4.67
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Authors' conclusions: After controlling for social desirability effects, negative perfectionism scores were found to correlate positively with disturbed eating attitudes scores, whereas positive perfectionism scores were found to be unrelated to disturbed eating attitude scores.
Limits: Focus only on rowing sample.
Perspectives:
This would suggest that resiliency against unhealthy eating could be increased by teaching athletes how to develop and maintain high levels of positive perfectionism. Intervention with goal in mind is a worthy topic for future research. 
Do these perfectionistic tendencies change throughout an athlete's career ? How and why do these changes occur ? What implications do these changes have on eating attitude ?
Sport_name_original: Rowing (i.e., Heavyweight and lightweight rowing)

Title: Perfectionism, social physique anxiety and disordered eating: a comparison of male and Female elite athletes
Authors: Haase, A.M., Prapavessis, H., Owens, G.
Inclusion criteria: Australian elite athletes
Mean_Age:
Males M=19.33, SD=4.07
Females M=18.54, SD=4.11
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Authors' conclusions: For both males and Females, negative perfectionism was moderately and positively correlated with SPA, while positive perfectionism was unrelated to SPA. For males athletes, negative perfectionism and SPA made no contribution to the prediction of disturbed eating attitudes. A mild inverse relationship was found between positive perfectionism and disturbed eating atitudes among male athletes.
Limits: N.A.
Perspectives: Further work is needed to clarify the directionality of relations between the individual difference variables used in the present study and disordered eating.

Title: Mental health symptoms related to body shape idealization in female fitness physique athletes
Authors: Mathisen, T.F., & Sundgot-Borgen, J.
Population subgroup:
Female fitness athletes (FA)
Recreationally active Female (FR)
T1 = pre-competition
T2 = at competition
T3 = post competition
Inclusion criteria: Participants fitness and body building athletes ; all responding Female fitness athletes planning to participate in the upcoming Norwegian competition period and initiating an energy restricted diet for such attendance, aged 18-40 years were included. Recreationally active Female at comparable age, with a body mass index of 18.5-35, and with no former of planned future experience with fitness or bodybuilding sports, or current profession as a personal trainer were included. For references athletes additional criterion was being recreationally physically active within any kind of sport/activity at least two times per week during the current year.
Mean_Age:
Female athletes M=28.4, SD=5.6
Female references M=30.2, SD=6
Mean_BMI:
Female athletes M=22.6, SD=2
Female references M=23.1, SD=2.8
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Authors' conclusions: We found correlations between self-oriented perfectionism and body image idealisation en fitness athletes, but not in Females references. This finding may be a potential moderator of how drive for leanness differentially correlates to ED, with more cognitive and eating restictions in fitness athletes and more uncontrolled and emotional eating in Females references.
Limits: Use of questionnaires developed and primarily validated for others populations samples (i.e., BES and TFE-Q for obese persons; CAPS for adolescents; DFL and DM for males), no clinical interviews and a short follow-up period.
Perspectives: N.A.

Title: Influence of perfectionism on variables associated to eating disorders in dance students
Authors: Arcelus, J., Garcia-Dantas, A., Sanchez-Martin, M., Del Rio, C.
Inclusion criteria: Female; aged 12-20; participation was voluntary; informed consent was obtained from their parents.
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Authors' conclusions: Body image has been found, not only to be a risk factor for the development of an ED, but as a mediator between perfectionism and dieting, and associated to performance cognitive anxiety which mediates the relationship between perfectionism and depression.
Limits: The use of general questionnaires such as the BDI II or EAT-26 which are not validated specifically to be used within the dance population, although they are validated and highly reliable measurements. Performance anxiety was measured hypothetically and it will be best to measure it previous to an event. Performance anxiety has been retrospectively measured instead of administering the questionnaires in situ before the performance.
Perspectives: Interventions aiming at reducing concern over mistakes may required a preventative component and by doing so it will help reducing body dissatisfaction, performance cognitive anxiety and dieting which will prevent the development of eating disorders in this vulnerable group. Future research should replicate this study and include males different age range, dance levels and nationalities.

Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Authors' conclusions: Body image has been found, not only to be a risk factor for the development of an ED, but as a mediator between perfectionism and dieting, and associated to performance cognitive anxiety which mediates the relationship between perfectionism and depression.
Limits: The use of general questionnaires such as the BDI II or EAT-26 which are not validated specifically to be used within the dance population, although they are validated and highly reliable measurements. Performance anxiety was measured hypothetically and it will be best to measure it previous to an event. Performance anxiety has been retrospectively measured instead of administering the questionnaires in situ before the performance.
Perspectives: Interventions aiming at reducing concern over mistakes may required a preventative component and by doing so it will help reducing body dissatisfaction, performance cognitive anxiety and dieting which will prevent the development of eating disorders in this vulnerable group. Future research should replicate this study and include males different age range, dance levels and nationalities.

Title: Eating attitudes, body appreciation, perfectionism, and the risk of exercise addiction in physically active adults: a cluster analysis
Authors: Piko, B.F., Berki, T.L., Kun, O., Mellor, D.
Inclusion criteria: 18 years of age and have an active lifestyle with regular physical activity (at least once a week, for a minimum of 30min)
Mean_Exercise frequency: 1h or less/week n=72 1-2h/week n=114 3-5h/week n=16 >5h/week n=3
Mean_Years of experience: 1 year or less n=40 2-3 years n=24 3-5 years n=17 5-10 years n=37 >10 years n=87
DEAB_measure: Validated Hungarian version of the Eating Attitude Test-26 (EAT-26)
Related_Factor_measure: Hungarian version of the Frost Multidimensional Perfectionism Scale (FMPS)
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Authors' conclusions: Exercise addiction (EA) can also occur in regular exercisers, not just athletes, and is often linked with disordered eating (DE) when body image concerns and perfectionism are present. These factors interact in complex ways, meaning EA is not always pathological but can signal risk when combined with unhealthy eating attitudes and excessive performance pressure
Limits: The cross-sectional design prevents causal conclusions, and reliance on self-reports, a relatively small and female-biased sample, and heterogeneous sport types limit generalizability
Perspectives: Future research should use larger, more diverse samples and longitudinal designs, while exploring additional psychological variables and protective factors to better understand and prevent EA and DE

Title: Disordered eating, perfectionism and body esteem on elite synchronized swimmers
Authors: Ferrand, C., Magnan, C., Rouveix, M., & Filaire, E.
Inclusion criteria: N.A.
DEAB_measure: The French Version of Dietary Restraint
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Authors' conclusions: Socially prescribed perfectionism did not explain variance in dietary restraint scores. Self esteem oriented perfectionism was associated with dietary restraint and was related to body dissatisfaction. The current findings show a mediating effect of body esteem weight satisfaction on the relationship between self-oriented perfectionism and dietary restraint. The perfectionist personality would be a contributing factor in dietary restraint required to maintin a low body weight.
Limits: Limitations of the study were linked to self-report measures and the cross-sectional nature of the investigations.
Perspectives: Future research is needed to gain a fuller understanding of the relationship between these three variable. The use of both self-report measures and interview formats in longitudinal studies must be developed to gain a more precise estimate of the nature and extent of inappropriate compensatory behaviours amog synchronized swimmers.

Title: Perfectionism and eating attitudes in competitive rowers: moderating effects of body mass, weight classification and gender
Authors: Haase, A.M., Prapavessis, H., & Owens, G.
Inclusion criteria: National level heavyweight and lightweight rowers from New Zealand and Australia
Mean_Age:
Female M=20.08, SD=4.23
Male M=21.49, SD=4.67
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Authors' conclusions: After controlling for social desirability effects, negative perfectionism scores were found to correlate positively with disturbed eating attitudes scores, whereas positive perfectionism scores were found to be unrelated to disturbed eating attitude scores.
Limits: Focus only on rowing sample.
Perspectives:
This would suggest that resiliency against unhealthy eating could be increased by teaching athletes how to develop and maintain high levels of positive perfectionism. Intervention with goal in mind is a worthy topic for future research. 
Do these perfectionistic tendencies change throughout an athlete's career ? How and why do these changes occur ? What implications do these changes have on eating attitude ?
Sport_name_original: Rowing (i.e., Heavyweight and lightweight rowing)

Population subgroup:
Female fitness athletes (FA)
Recreationally active Female (FR)
T1 = pre-competition
T2 = at competition
T3 = post competition
Inclusion criteria: Participants fitness and body building athletes ; all responding Female fitness athletes planning to participate in the upcoming Norwegian competition period and initiating an energy restricted diet for such attendance, aged 18-40 years were included. Recreationally active Female at comparable age, with a body mass index of 18.5-35, and with no former of planned future experience with fitness or bodybuilding sports, or current profession as a personal trainer were included. For references athletes additional criterion was being recreationally physically active within any kind of sport/activity at least two times per week during the current year.
Mean_Age:
Female athletes M=28.4, SD=5.6
Female references M=30.2, SD=6
Mean_BMI:
Female athletes M=22.6, SD=2
Female references M=23.1, SD=2.8
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Authors' conclusions: We found correlations between self-oriented perfectionism and body image idealisation en fitness athletes, but not in Females references. Limits: Use of questionnaires developed and primarily validated for others populations samples (i.e., BES and TFE-Q for obese persons; CAPS for adolescents; DFL and DM for males), no clinical interviews and a short follow-up period.
Perspectives: N.A.

Title: Eating attitudes, body appreciation, perfectionism, and the risk of exercise addiction in physically active adults: a cluster analysis
Authors: Piko, B.F., Berki, T.L., Kun, O., Mellor, D.
Inclusion criteria: 18 years of age and have an active lifestyle with regular physical activity (at least once a week, for a minimum of 30min)
Mean_Exercise frequency: 1h or less/week n=72 1-2h/week n=114 3-5h/week n=16 >5h/week n=3
Mean_Years of experience: 1 year or less n=40 2-3 years n=24 3-5 years n=17 5-10 years n=37 >10 years n=87
DEAB_measure: Validated Hungarian version of the Eating Attitude Test-26 (EAT-26)
Related_Factor_measure: Hungarian version of the Frost Multidimensional Perfectionism Scale (FMPS)
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Authors' conclusions: Exercise addiction (EA) can also occur in regular exercisers, not just athletes, and is often linked with disordered eating (DE) when body image concerns and perfectionism are present. These factors interact in complex ways, meaning EA is not always pathological but can signal risk when combined with unhealthy eating attitudes and excessive performance pressure
Limits: The cross-sectional design prevents causal conclusions, and reliance on self-reports, a relatively small and female-biased sample, and heterogeneous sport types limit generalizability
Perspectives: Future research should use larger, more diverse samples and longitudinal designs, while exploring additional psychological variables and protective factors to better understand and prevent EA and DE

Title: Perfectionism and learning experiences in dance class as risk factors for eating disorders in dancers
Authors: Penniment, K.J., & Egan, S.J.
Inclusion criteria: Being a Female aged between 18 and 30 years, currently studying classical and/or jazz ballet
Mean_BMI: 22.5% may be classified as underweight, with a BMI under 18.5kg/m²
Sporting population: 20.4% reported that they had danced semi professionally at one time, and 23.9% reported that they had danced at a professional level at one time.
Mean_Years of experience:
Dance tuition M=6.92, SD=22
Years studying dance M=14.5, SD=5.90
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Authors' conclusions: The relation between perfectionism and eating disorders symptoms was partially mediated by thinness related learning. The hypothesis that the relationship between thinness related learning and eating disorders symptoms were partially mediated by thiness restricting expectancies was also supported. A direct relationship between perfectionism and eating disorders symptoms was found.
Limits: The data was cross sectional. Although the current model fit the data well, there are multiple other risk factors for ED and it is very likely that this risk is determined by multiple factors and is not simply a function of the emphasis on thinness in the dance environment, or perfectionism. The sample was too small to split into professional and non professional dancers to examine if the model was the same in these groups. Our view of perfectionism was aligned with the construct of clinical perfectionism, and as a result we examined a selected subset of scales from the FMPS and did not use relevant scales from the HMPS.
Perspectives:
It would be useful for future research to examine the efficacy of targeting young Female involved in dance with elevated levels of perfectionism for prevention programs, as preliminary findings are positive for the ability of programs targeting perfectionism to reduce eating disorders risk in Female adolescents. 
It would be useful for clinicians to consider directly targeting perfectionism through CBT programs for perfectionism in young Female involved in dance classes as it is likely to be a factor that puts them at higher risk of developing an eating disorders within this environment.

Title: Eating attitudes, body appreciation, perfectionism, and the risk of exercise addiction in physically active adults: a cluster analysis
Authors: Piko, B.F., Berki, T.L., Kun, O., Mellor, D.
Inclusion criteria: 18 years of age and have an active lifestyle with regular physical activity (at least once a week, for a minimum of 30min)
Mean_Exercise frequency: 1h or less/week n=72 1-2h/week n=114 3-5h/week n=16 >5h/week n=3
Mean_Years of experience: 1 year or less n=40 2-3 years n=24 3-5 years n=17 5-10 years n=37 >10 years n=87
Related_Factor_measure: Hungarian version of the Frost Multidimensional Perfectionism Scale (FMPS)
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Authors' conclusions: Exercise addiction (EA) can also occur in regular exercisers, not just athletes, and is often linked with disordered eating (DE) when body image concerns and perfectionism are present. Limits: The cross-sectional design prevents causal conclusions, and reliance on self-reports, a relatively small and female-biased sample, and heterogeneous sport types limit generalizability
Perspectives: Future research should use larger, more diverse samples and longitudinal designs, while exploring additional psychological variables and protective factors to better understand and prevent EA and DE

Title: Application of the transdiagnostic cognitive-behavioral model of eating disorders to the athletic population
Authors: Shanmugam, V., Jowett, S., & Meyer, C.
Inclusion criteria: Males and Females British athletes
Sporting population: 31% elite athletes competing at the international or national level, 69% non elite competing for county/regional, 20% club and 30% university teams
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Authors' conclusions: Avoidant attachmalet was associated with poor quality relationships with their influential parent and principal coach. Athletes who experiencd more conflict in their relationships were more likely to criticize themselves, which in turn can be related to low self esteem, with athletes feeling unvalued and worthless as indivdiuals. Subsequently, low self esteem was linked to higher depressive symptoms, which in turn was lined to eating psychopathology. Self critical perfectionism may play a more pivotal role in eating psychopathology than personal standard perfectionism. The possession of high self imposed standards may not be related to eating psychopathology. The psychopathological process of perfectionism and self esteem both seem to exert an indirect effect on eating psychopathology, while depression exerts a direct effect.
Limits: The study was cross sectional. There are some limitations related to the operational definitions and measurement of the constructs related to the transdiagnostic cognitive behavioral model. In this study only one aspect of the concept of mood intolerance was captured. The current study employed self report measures, results are subject to social desirability and acquiescence response bias. The study did not use a control group of non athletes and a sample of athletes with eating disorders. It therefore remains unclear whether the relationships observed would extend to the nonathletic population or to clinical populations.
Perspectives: Continuing to develop a more encompassing understanding of the risk factors associated with eating disorders in athletes (e.g., examining psycho-social risk factors in addition to the sport-specific risk factors) wa may come a step closer in being able to prevent, manage and treat the disorder within the broader sporting community.

Title: The role of division III sports participation in the relationship between perfectionism and disordered eating symptomatology
Authors: Somasundaram, P., & Burgess, A.M.
Population subgroup:
204 Non-athletes
44 Aesthetic athletes
230 Team/individual sport athletes
Inclusion criteria: Female undergraduate students from six liberal arts colleges in the Northeast region of the United States of America.
Mean_Age:
Aesthetic M=19.26, SD=1.11
Inidvidual/teams M=19.24, SD=1.15
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Authors' conclusions: Results indicated a moderate, positive and significant relationship between evaluative concerns and disordered eating. The associations of striving with the dimensions of eating psychopathology were both weak and one was non-significant. For each group, evaluative concerns was found to have a significant, positive association with the EAT and EDI-BD. Team/individuals athletes have significant positive associations between evaluative concerns and eating/body attitudes while aesthetic athletes had non-significant association between these variables. Regarding striving, team/indivdiual athletes maintained marginally-significant relationships between this dimension of perfectionism and the EAT, while aesthetic athletes maintained a non-significant association between the two variables. There is no relationship between striving and body dissatisfaction for team/indivdiual athletes. Aesthetic athletes displayed a significant negative association between striving and EDI-BD.
Limits: The data was collected exclusively at colleges with an NCAA Division III program. This lower level of competition may have affected the results. The sample size was small.
Perspectives: Future studies may replicate the current methods aong a more competitive population as the degree of competitiveness enforced and internalized by athletes has been highlighted as an important predictor for the development of maladaptive psychological symptoms.

Title: Prevalence and correlates of disordered eating in Female figure skaters
Authors: Voelker, D.K., Gould, D., Reel, J.J.
Inclusion criteria: Female figure skaters aged 12 to 25. Former skaters, basic skills skaters, and those in adult skating programs (e.g., age-based competitions following adult test equivalencies) were excluded
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Authors' conclusions: All sport related weight pressures were significantly related to disordered eating, however only self consciousness of weight and appearance emerged as a significant correlate in the regression model. Body dissatisfaction explained an additional 5.7% of the variance in disordered eating. Sport related body dissatisfaction also emerged as a significant predictor. Positive perfectionism made a significant contribution, but negative perfectionism did not. Self esteem may not be strongly related to disordered eating. Athletic identity did not emerge as a significant variable in the final regression model, although the bivariate correlation indicated a significant positive relationship with disordered eating.
Limits: Societal weight pressures were not exmained. Self report nature of the surveys and the willingness of athletes to honestly and accurately respond to survey items. The results are also based on a conveniance sample of skaters limited to clubs in the Midwest and Northeast. Cross sectional design, causal relationships and change over time could not be determined.
Perspectives:
Sport psychology practiitioners should aid this effort by teaching skaters to appreciate body strengths and utilize psychological skills that may buffer the impact of negative weight pressures (e.g., utilizing positive self talk and realistic goal-setting). 
A random and more representative sample of skaters nationally and internationally, inclusive of males, should be considered in future research.
Sport_name_original: Figure skating (singles, multiple, synchronized, ice dancing, pairs)

Title: Muscle dysmorphia and its associated psychological features in three groups of recreational athletes
Authors: Cerea, S., Bottesi, G., Pacelli, Q.F., Paoli, A., & Ghisi, M.
Population subgroup:
42 Bodybuilders (BB group) 
61 Strenght athletes (SA group)
22 Fitness practitioners (FP group)
Inclusion criteria: At least 18 years of age; absence of severe neurological or medical conditions; no current or past psychothic disorders; no evidence of intellectual disabilities; Italian athletes who trained regularly for recreational purposes: bodybuilders, strenght training athletes, and fitness practitioners.
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Authors' conclusions: Self esteem is significaltly related to muscle dysmorphia. Perfectionism is non-significantly related to MD. Perfectionism socially prescribed is significantly related to MD among bodybuilders. Social phobia is significantly related to MD. Orthorexia is significantly related to MD among bodybuilders. Depression is significantly related to MD.
Limits: First the sample size was relativelly small which likely reduces the generalizability of our conclusions. Related to this issue, the statisticcal power of the employed regression design could not guarantee a reliable detection of MD predictors. Secondly, the online recruitmalet strategy we adopted under-sampled those without internet capability and prevented the opportunity of conducting face-to-face interviews of participants self-identified as recreational bodybuilders and recreational strength athletess. Lastly, the absence of psychometric information for the MPS is another limitation.
Perspectives: Improving the identification of predictors and risk factors for MD, as well as its associated psychological features, might facilitate the identification of at-risk trainers, as well as the development of prevention strategies and interventions. Furthermore, a deeper understanding of MD manifestation among athletes may help to distinguishing individuals participating in a healthy manner versus those participating in an unhealthy manner.
Sport_name_original: Bodybuilding, strength training, fitness

Title: Disordered eating attitudes, anxiety, self esteem and perfectionism in young athletes and non athletes
Authors: Petisco-Rodriguez, C., Sanchez-Sanchez, L.C., Fernandez-Garcia, R., Sanchez-Sanchez, J., & Garcia-Montes, J.M.
Journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
Population subgroup:
40 Athletes competing in rhythmic gymnastics
40 Athletes competing in football
40 Non-athletes
Inclusion criteria: Membership in Spanish sport clubs or rhythmic gymnastics, or footballers with a background > 4 years of systematic training and competitive experience, training a minimum of 8h per week, with absence of severe injuries
Mean_Age:
Gymnasts M=16.6, SD=2.62
Footballers M=17.98, SD=3.42
Mean_BMI:
M=20.63, SD=2.77
Gymnasts M=18.72, SD=1.54
Footballers M=22.45, SD=2.93
Sporting population: Gymnasts group consisted of 5 elite competing internationally and 35 at the national level
Range_Exercise frequency:
Elites : 20-35h per week
National gymnasts : 12-20h per week
Footballers : 4 training sessions plus a competitive match per week
Range_Years of experience: Minimum 4 years of training and competitive experience
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Authors' conclusions: Correlation obtained between anxiety (both trait and state) and the EAT-40 was positively and statistically significant. In the multiple regression analysis that was performed with SCOFF scores as a dependent variable, the most predictive variable was socially prescribed perfectionism. It showed negative correlation with EAT-40 and self esteem. Self esteem is probably a protective factor to develop an eating disorder despite perfectionism, which is the most predictive variable as the multiple linear regression showed, and this variable was high in athletes.
Limits: Small sample size. No precise clinical diagnostic data were available to validate ED screening in the current study.
Perspectives:
In the future, the use of other kinds of measurements, less subjected to the desirability bias, would help to discriminate whether the improvements in self-esteem and eating disorders in elite gymnasts are due to this bias or to preventing psychological treatments and trainings by coaches.
 In addition, it is important to further explore the impact of other psychological factors on eating disordered behaviours such as body image, mood, depression or motivation, among others; due to the fact that they imply multifactorial aetiology of disorders.

Title: Perfectionism and eating psychopathology among dancers: the role of high standards and self-criticism
Authors: Goodwin, H., Arcelus, J., Geach, N., & Meyer, C.
Inclusion criteria: Female; aged 18 years or older; current member of a university recreational dance club; clubs comprised ballet, modern, tap, jazz, and/or hi hop disciplines. The participants were not screened for previous or current eating disorder treatment.
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Authors' conclusions: High standards and self criticism are positively associated with eating restraint, eating concern, weight concern and shape concern. The associations between self-criticism and eating pathology were not moderated by high standards. Self criticism fully mediated the relationships between high standards and restraint, eating concern, weight concern and shape concern.
Limits: The self report nature of the data means reports may be unreliable and subject to social desirability bias. The method of participants recruitlent precluded any analysis of response rate, and it was not known whether or not there was a bias to those who chose to participate versus those who did not participate. The heterogeneous nature of the sample means that underlying group differences (between dance style, competency level and hours of dance practice) may have been missed.
Perspectives: The relationships between high standards, self-criticism and eating disorder risk requires examination in more homogenous sub-groups of dancers, to further identify the risk environments for eating psychopathology.

Mean_Age:
Female M=20.08, SD=4.23
Male M=21.49, SD=4.67
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Authors' conclusions: After controlling for social desirability effects, negative perfectionism scores were found to correlate positively with disturbed eating attitudes scores, whereas positive perfectionism scores were found to be unrelated to disturbed eating attitude scores.

Title: Comparing population-general and sport-specific correlates of disordered eating amongst elite athletes: a cross-sectional study
Authors: Fatt, S.J., George, E., Hay, P., Jeacocke, N., & Mitchison, D.
Inclusion criteria: Current and former athletes, who had competed at thenational, international, professional or NCAA Division I level
Related_Factor: Athletes perceptions of power balances with their coach/training staff
Related_Factor_measure: Modified version of the Participative decision-making subscale of the Empowering Leadership Questionnaire (ELQ-PD)
Related_Factor_CLASS: Interpersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Athletes perceptions of power balances with their coach/training staff
Authors' conclusions: Both population-general and athlete-specific factors have independent associations with disordered eating, including pressures (pressures for thinness and weight-loss from within sport) and psychological processes (drive for thinness, drive for leanness for performance, and athletic identity).
Limits: The cross sectional design ; athletes were a self-selected sample, likely leading to a bias in our sample towards participants who were interested in body image, eating and exercise ; the sample primarily included Australian female athletes ; over 2000 suspected illegitimate spam responses were removed from the study.
Perspectives: Several findings have previously indicated small but significant effects of greater risk for athletes competing in lean versus non-lean sports, this was not replicated in the present study. This challenges notions of at-risk athletes archetypes (e.g., female athletes participating in lean sport) and narrow views of eating disorder symptomatology (e.g., low BMI, vomiting) encouraging broader screening for disodered eating accross entire athlete populations. Sporting organisations should develop and implement policies for managing athletes al all levels of risk, including primary, secondary, and tertiary interventions.

Mean_BMI:

Ballet non elite Female M=19.04, SD=2.26
Gymnasts elite male M=21.83, SD=2.26
Gymnasts elite Female M=20.16, SD=1.99
Gymnasts non elite male M=21.43, SD=3.29
Gymnasts non elite Female M=19.94, SD=2.42
Sporting population:
Elite dancers (N=66)
Recreational dancers (N=47)
International competition gymnasts (N=69)
Non elite gymnasts (N=67)
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Attitudinal dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: Social pressure, social support, self esteem, body dissatisfaction was related to DE. Social support was not strongly related to DE.. Activity specific body image dissatisfaction is a better predictor of DE than general body image dissatisfaction. When the pressure to be thin was introduced into the model, the competitive level was no longer significant in predicting aesthetic performers DE. Our final model explained 61% of the variance in aesthetic performers disordered eating and also confirmed the role of low self esteem and specific body image dissatisfaction as partial mediators from pressure to be thin to DE.
Limits: Small size of the groups of male aesthetic performers, and the absence of a group of non elite male ballet dancers. The cross sectional design does not allow for full comprehension of the relationship between participation in these activities and the development of disordered eating. The use of self-report questionnaires and the fact that we have not taken into account the percentage of respondents and non respondents.
Perspectives: It is important to distinguish between pressure on Female and male aesthetic performers. Such preventative measures are essential in professional dancer schools and especially gymnastics clubs. These actions should focus on promoting young aesthetic performer's self-esteem and satisfaction with their activity specific body image, which is essential to reducing the impact of pressure to be thin on their eating and weight control behaviors. Title: Psychosocial risk factors of bulimic symptomatology among Female athletes
Authors: Greenleaf, C., Petrie, T., Reel, J., & Carter, J.
Inclusion criteria: NCAA Divisions I Female collegiate athletes drawn from three universities located in the Midwest, Soutwest, and Mountain regions of the United States.
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Attitudinal dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: The inclusion of each set of variables (internalization, body dissatisfaction, dietary intent, and negative affect) contributed significantly to the prediction of bulimic symptomatology, accounting for 42% of the variance. Only higher levels of body dissatifaction, a greater focus on diet and restricting food intake, and stronger feelings of guilt were related significantly to BULIT-R scores.
Limits: All the data collected were self reported and susceptible to socially desirable responding. The racial/ethnic makeup of the sample; our sample was predominantly Caucasian, thus limiting the generalizability to similar samples of Female college athletes. The cross sectional design of the study does not allow for the determination of the temporal nature of the relationships between psychosocial variables and bulimic symptoms.
Perspectives:
Use prospective design. 
Research can be advanced by improving measurement of affect, to capture temporal ebb and flow of mood as it relates to eating attitudes and behaviors.

Title: Eating disorders in Taekwondo athletes: the contribution of coach behavior, body satisfaction, and goal orientation
Authors: Baric, R., Erdeljac, T.
Inclusion criteria: Active practice of Taekwondo for at least 6 months and being a competitor in one of three competities categories: cadets, junior athletes or senior athletes
Sporting population:
17.3% top elite athletes, members of national selection and elite athletes
25 elite male
33 elite female
107 non-elite male
170 non-elite female
DEAB_measure: Croatian version of the Eating Attitudes Test (EAT_26)
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Attitudinal dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: Goal orientation, body dissatisfaction, and negative behavior and pressure from coaches significantly contribute to the risk of ED development in female and male cadet, junior and non-elite athletes, while body dissatisfaction seems to be the strongest predictor, especially in female athletes.
Limits: The sample size, although it is realistic in relation to the number of active taekwondo competitors in Croatia. Self reported questionnaires.
Perspectives: Including other measures, more adjusted to male ED symptoms. As the results showed the significance of the behavior of coaches in relation to athletes ED symptoms, it would be very interesting to investigate the transgenerational transfer of distorted values, beliefs and behaviors related to ED from coaches to athletes, i.e., to investigate coaches history of ED symptoms and their current behavior.

Title: Investigation of the relationship between muscle dysmorphia disorder, orthorexia nervosa, and motivation in male individuals engaged in bodybuilding sports
Authors: Abraş, H., Erdag, D., Buran, A.
Journal: Cyprus Turkish Journal of Psychiatry & Psychology
Inclusion criteria: Volunteer male participants aged between 18 and 58 engaged in bodybuilding; registered in gyms in TRNC.
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Attitudinal dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: As muscle dysmorphia increases, orthorexia nervosa increases in individuals engaged in bodybuilding sports in the TRNC.
Limits: Since this study was conducted only on male bodybuilders, the findings cannot be generalized to Female bodybuilders.
Perspectives:
It is essential to provide education on muscle dysmorphia, orthorexia nervosa, and the use of ergogenic nutritional supplements in Physical Education and Sports Schools, as well as in coach training programs. Additionally, training on athlete nutrition and sports psychology in these institutions would equip them with knowledge about both athlete motivations and the mental health disorders frequently seen in athletes. Given the rise of these mental health issues in gyms, sports psychologists should be present in these environments, and mental health assessments should be conducted alongside medical evaluations for new memberships.
Conducting similar studies across different sports and with female participants could contribute valuable new insights to the literature.

Title: Body Talk, Athletic Identity, and Eating Disorder Symptoms in male
Authors: Ahlich, E., Choquette, E.M., Rancourt, D.
Inclusion criteria: 18-49 years; recruited using convenience sampling from a large southeastern university's research; receiving research credit upon completion of the study; informed consent
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Attitudinal dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: The current findings support body talk and fat talk as a potential risk factor for eating disorders among male. Muscle-focused body talk may not a risk factor for diagnostic eating disorder symptoms. Muscle talk among male is related less to muscle dissatisfaction and more to male socioalization processes. Athletic identity did non emerge as a significant moderator of the association between body talk and eating disorder symptoms.
Limits: The study was limited to a single university campus in the southeastern United States, limiting generalizability of the findings. Few participants endorsed aesthetic or lean sports, potentially attenuating results.
Perspectives:
Future work may benefit from using a more objective of body composition. 
Future work should explore such associations among male in a clinical sample, examining whether fat or muscle talk is associated with eating disorder and/or muscle dysmorphia symptom severity. 
Fat talk may be an important prevention target amon male, regardless of athletic identity.
