Title: Overweight preoccupation is associated with eating pathology in male collegiate athletes with body dissatisfaction
Authors: Murray, M.F., Perelman, H., Sandhu, D., Quinones, I.C., & Haedt-Matt, A.A.
Inclusion criteria: Collegiate athletes who identified as male and members of university-sponsored varsity athletic teams; were over age 18 years, and endorsed body dissatisfaction (i.e., scores greater than 1 on the overweight preoccupation or appearance orientation subscales of the multidimensional body self relations questionnaire, or scores greater than 5 on the appearance orientation subscales)
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perceptual dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: This studies clarifies notable correlates, particularly overweight preoccupation, of eating pathology in male athletes and highlights sport confidence as a potential prevention and intervention target.
Limits: Causality cannot be inffered from cross sectional findings and the causality of risk factors for eating pathology in male athletes remains unclear. Internal consistency of the purging subscale of the EPSI was poor. Alternately, the items composing this subscale may not adequately reflect compensatory purging behaviors or its underlying motivations in this population.
Perspectives: Future research would benefit from a larger sample without preset body dissatisfaction criteria to ensure adequate power for moderation, to allow for direct comparison across sport types, positions, and competition levels, and to avoid potential floor effects. More longitudinal and mediational designs are needed to model how sport related pressures relate to these varied correlates.

Perspectives: Future research would need to implement longitudinal designs in order to determine the specific directions of the relationships examined. Replicate the study with larger more representative samples and utilizing different recruitmalet techniques.

Title: Psychosocial risk factors of bulimic symptomatology among Female athletes
Authors: Greenleaf, C., Petrie, T., Reel, J., & Carter, J.
Inclusion criteria: NCAA Divisions I Female collegiate athletes drawn from three universities located in the Midwest, Soutwest, and Mountain regions of the United States.
Related_Factor_measure: Multidimensional Body Self Relations Questionnaire-Appearance Evaluation (MBSRQ-AE)
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perceptual dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: The inclusion of each set of variables (internalization, body dissatisfaction, dietary intent, and negative affect) contributed significantly to the prediction of bulimic symptomatology, accounting for 42% of the variance. Only higher levels of body dissatifaction, a greater focus on diet and restricting food intake, and stronger feelings of guilt were related significantly to BULIT-R scores.
Limits: All the data collected were self reported and susceptible to socially desirable responding. The racial/ethnic makeup of the sample; our sample was predominantly Caucasian, thus limiting the generalizability to similar samples of Female college athletes. The cross sectional design of the study does not allow for the determination of the temporal nature of the relationships between psychosocial variables and bulimic symptoms.
Perspectives:

Title: Individual differences in male body image: an examination of self-objectivation in recreational body builders
Authors: Hallsworth, L., Wade, T., Tiggemann, M.
Inclusion criteria: Males. The first group consisted of bodybuilders; minimum level of training twice a week for at least a year. The second group consisted of competitive weightlifters recruited from the state weightlifting associations in four states of Australia.
Mean_Age:
Bodybuilders M=28.89, SD=6.19
Weightlifters M=27.60, SD=8.70
Non-athletic control M=26.43, SD=8.15
Mean_BMI:
Weightlifters M=28.60, SD=6.90
Bodybuilders M=26.04, SD=3.08
Controls M=24.18, SD=2.80
Mean_Exercise frequency:
Bodybuilders M=6.40 hours per week
Weightlifters M=12.12 hours per week 
Controls M=3.8 hours per week
Mean_Years of experience:
Bodybuilders M=6.14 years
Weightlifters M=9.06 years
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perceptual dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: Bodybuilding may represent a practice that encourages male to become more self-conscious of their bodies, putting them at greater risk of experiencing greater levels of monitoring of body appearance and anxiety about physical appearance. This body self consciousness is associated with a greater risk of body dissatisfaction and drive for muscularity. Weightlifting does not appear to represent an objectifying climate.
Limits: The cross sectional nature makes it possible only to speculate on the directions of causality. Unequal sample sizes of groups in our analyses, particularly with respect to fewer competitive weightlifters. Unknown selection bias that may be operating in the bodybuilder and weightlifter groups, and any subsequent influence on the interpretation of our results. The weighlifting and bodybuilder groups differed not only in the nature of their sport, but also in competitive nature of this sport, which may introduce confound for differences found between the groups.
Perspectives: Health pursuits for male should emphasize achievement and function rather than appearance if they are to avoid deleterious consesquences.

Title: Link between eating disorder risk, self-esteem and body image among Puerto Rican high school student-athletes
Authors: Ayala, R.V.
Journal: Journal of Physical Education and Sport
Country:
United States of America
Puerto Rico
Inclusion criteria: Student-athletes from three different academic institutions in Puerto Rico; current high school student-athlete
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perceptual dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: No relationship between self-esteem, body image, and eating disorders risk. No significant correlations were found between the independent variables and eating disorder risk, and the independant variables did not predict eating disorder risk.
Limits:
Awareness of the study could have biased the participant's reponses.
There was not an equal representation of gender since most of participants were males. 
The possibility of students being fearful exposing low self-esteem, negative body image, and/or eating disorder risk. 
Small sample size and low response rate, which was less than 30%. 
Lack of a control group due to time constraints and resources.
Perspectives:
Athletic departments should create preventive programs for the student-athletes. Schools should have health care professionals available for student-athletes to avoid future problems with eating disorders, self-esteem and body image. Also having a thorough physical and psychological examination of student-athletes before participation in sports is a great way to screen for possible needs. Athletic director and coaches can assist the student using a non-judgemntal approach to connect them with the most appropriate help. Athletics directors need to understand eating disorders, self-esteem, and body image. 
Academics could focus on conducted studies with other ethnic populations and use different variables in a much larger sample size. More psychosocial variables can be studied to analyze different correlations. Some of these variables might include gender, sports played, social media influence, coach's coaching style or method, and peer and parental influence, among others. A imilar representations of males and Females is also needed to analyze the differences between genders. Future research could focus on different parts of the Island, including the rural and uran areas. In addition, using a mixted methods intervention could provide more insight. Future research could conduct a more thorough analysis to obtain both quantitative and qualitative data.  In addition, it would e valuable to include a control group to compare student-athletes ith non-student-athletes. Finally a longitudinal study could be performed to examine eating disorder risk in student-athletes from high school to college.

Related_Factor_measure: Factor 3 includes: I would like my clothes to fit better; I would like my physique to be different; I would like to be thinner
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perceptual dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: The result of the linear regression clearly shows that the most significant explanatory weight is given by dissatisfaction with body image, despite the normal weight found. Social networks do not show a significant relationship with the risk of developing ED. We found a relationship between the risk of manifesting ED and feeling fatigued, getting little rest, and having problems concentrating. Fatigue and the risk of developing ED are not related to the hours of sports practice.
Limits: First, the sampling is not random and therefore does not offer representative data for each group of athletes. Second, there may be non-observational errors due to the impossibility of obtaining all the influencial variables, such as psychological variables. Third, although the survey were short, they were adiministered while medical examinations were conducted, meaning the subjects attitudes and cooperation could be rushed or hasty. Fourth, BMI is not a completely objective tool for diagnosing normal weight, underweight or overweight, particularly in the athletic population, since this value only considers weight and height, discarding other helpful information such as muscle mass and its ratio to fat mass. Even within the group of athletes, it is recommaleded to differentiate according to modality for diagnosis, prevention and intervention. Title: Overweight preoccupation is associated with eating pathology in male collegiate athletes with body dissatisfaction
Authors: Murray, M.F., Perelman, H., Sandhu, D., Quinones, I.C., & Haedt-Matt, A.A.
Inclusion criteria: Collegiate athletes who identified as male and members of university-sponsored varsity athletic teams; were over age 18 years, and endorsed body dissatisfaction (i.e., scores greater than 1 on the overweight preoccupation or appearance orientation subscales of the multidimensional body self relations questionnaire, or scores greater than 5 on the appearance orientation subscales)
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perceptual dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: This studies clarifies notable correlates, particularly overweight preoccupation, of eating pathology in male athletes and highlights sport confidence as a potential prevention and intervention target.
Limits: Causality cannot be inffered from cross sectional findings and the causality of risk factors for eating pathology in male athletes remains unclear. Internal consistency of the purging subscale of the EPSI was poor. Alternately, the items composing this subscale may not adequately reflect compensatory purging behaviors or its underlying motivations in this population.
Perspectives: Future research would benefit from a larger sample without preset body dissatisfaction criteria to ensure adequate power for moderation, to allow for direct comparison across sport types, positions, and competition levels, and to avoid potential floor effects. More longitudinal and mediational designs are needed to model how sport related pressures relate to these varied correlates.

Inclusion criteria: Collegiate athletes who identified as male and members of university-sponsored varsity athletic teams; were over age 18 years, and endorsed body dissatisfaction (i.e., scores greater than 1 on the overweight preoccupation or appearance orientation subscales of the multidimensional body self relations questionnaire, or scores greater than 5 on the appearance orientation subscales)
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perceptual dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: This studies clarifies notable correlates, particularly overweight preoccupation, of eating pathology in male athletes and highlights sport confidence as a potential prevention and intervention target.
Limits: Causality cannot be inffered from cross sectional findings and the causality of risk factors for eating pathology in male athletes remains unclear. Internal consistency of the purging subscale of the EPSI was poor. Alternately, the items composing this subscale may not adequately reflect compensatory purging behaviors or its underlying motivations in this population.
Perspectives: Future research would benefit from a larger sample without preset body dissatisfaction criteria to ensure adequate power for moderation, to allow for direct comparison across sport types, positions, and competition levels, and to avoid potential floor effects. More longitudinal and mediational designs are needed to model how sport related pressures relate to these varied correlates.

Title: Psychosocial correlates of disordered eating among male collegiate athletes
Authors: Petrie, T.A., Greenleaf, C., Carter, J.E., & Reel, J.J.
Population subgroup:
Asymptomatic group based on their QEDD responses (n=164)
Symptomatic group based on their QEDD responses (n=35)
Inclusion criteria: Male collegiate athletes from three different NCAA division I institutions located in the Midwest, Southwest and Mountain regions of the US
Mean_Years of experience:
College level M=1.81, SD=1.30
M=8.70, SD=5.28
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perceptual dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: The psychosocial factors generally were unrelated to level of eating pathology. The male athletes were healthy in terms of their eating behaviors, had few negative mood concerns, were moderately satisfied with their bodies and experienced few pressures from personal and societal sources to change their weight or body size/shape.
Limits: Negative mood was represented by a single-item measures, this may have affected the relationship with disordered eating. All data are based on athlete self report and thus are subject to mono-method bias as well as underreporting that might occur when assessing sensitive areas. Only two of the male athletes were classified as having an eating disorder and both had an ED-NOS.
Perspectives: Researchers should use measures of specific mood states (e.g., depression, anxiety) that are based on multiple items (e.g., PANAS-X), include measures of positive mood state (e.g., optimism, happiness, confidence) and incorporate designs (e.g., longitudinal) that allow these questions to be addressed directly. Professionals should be attuned to looking for subclinical level presentations of symptoms among the athletes with whom they work. Professionals may want to work proactively with male athletic teams, educating them about healthy, nutritional eating and maintaing regular exercise during the off-season. Such approaches may assist male collegiate athletes during the shift from the structural regimen that occurs when in-season and the potentially more relaxed, self-initiated approach that is taken during the off season.
Sport_name_original: Football; basketball; cheerleading; cross-country; diving; fencing; golf; gymnastics; ice hockey; lacrosse; swimming; tennis; track and field; volleyball; cross-country skiing; alpine skiing

Title: Overweight preoccupation is associated with eating pathology in male collegiate athletes with body dissatisfaction
Authors: Murray, M.F., Perelman, H., Sandhu, D., Quinones, I.C., & Haedt-Matt, A.A.
Inclusion criteria: Collegiate athletes who identified as male and members of university-sponsored varsity athletic teams; were over age 18 years, and endorsed body dissatisfaction (i.e., scores greater than 1 on the overweight preoccupation or appearance orientation subscales of the multidimensional body self relations questionnaire, or scores greater than 5 on the appearance orientation subscales)
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perceptual dimension of body image and self-esteem
Related_Factor_sub-class 3: Judgement of size, shape and weight
Authors' conclusions: This studies clarifies notable correlates, particularly overweight preoccupation, of eating pathology in male athletes and highlights sport confidence as a potential prevention and intervention target.
Limits: Causality cannot be inffered from cross sectional findings and the causality of risk factors for eating pathology in male athletes remains unclear. Internal consistency of the purging subscale of the EPSI was poor. Alternately, the items composing this subscale may not adequately reflect compensatory purging behaviors or its underlying motivations in this population.
Perspectives: Future research would benefit from a larger sample without preset body dissatisfaction criteria to ensure adequate power for moderation, to allow for direct comparison across sport types, positions, and competition levels, and to avoid potential floor effects. More longitudinal and mediational designs are needed to model how sport related pressures relate to these varied correlates.

Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perceptual dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: Perfectionism in athletes is linked to higher stress, eating disturbances, and body perception issues, with women showing higher stress, emotional eating, and restrictive eating behaviors. Title: Psychosocial correlates of disordered eating among male collegiate athletes
Authors: Petrie, T.A., Greenleaf, C., Carter, J.E., & Reel, J.J.
Population subgroup:
Asymptomatic group based on their QEDD responses (n=164)
Symptomatic group based on their QEDD responses (n=35)
Inclusion criteria: Male collegiate athletes from three different NCAA division I institutions located in the Midwest, Southwest and Mountain regions of the US
Mean_Years of experience:
College level M=1.81, SD=1.30
M=8.70, SD=5.28
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perceptual dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: The psychosocial factors generally were unrelated to level of eating pathology. The male athletes were healthy in terms of their eating behaviors, had few negative mood concerns, were moderately satisfied with their bodies and experienced few pressures from personal and societal sources to change their weight or body size/shape.
Limits: Negative mood was represented by a single-item measures, this may have affected the relationship with disordered eating. All data are based on athlete self report and thus are subject to mono-method bias as well as underreporting that might occur when assessing sensitive areas. Only two of the male athletes were classified as having an eating disorder and both had an ED-NOS.
Perspectives: Researchers should use measures of specific mood states (e.g., depression, anxiety) that are based on multiple items (e.g., PANAS-X), include measures of positive mood state (e.g., optimism, happiness, confidence) and incorporate designs (e.g., longitudinal) that allow these questions to be addressed directly. Professionals should be attuned to looking for subclinical level presentations of symptoms among the athletes with whom they work. Professionals may want to work proactively with male athletic teams, educating them about healthy, nutritional eating and maintaing regular exercise during the off-season. Such approaches may assist male collegiate athletes during the shift from the structural regimen that occurs when in-season and the potentially more relaxed, self-initiated approach that is taken during the off season.

Title: Overweight preoccupation is associated with eating pathology in male collegiate athletes with body dissatisfaction
Authors: Murray, M.F., Perelman, H., Sandhu, D., Quinones, I.C., & Haedt-Matt, A.A.
Inclusion criteria: Collegiate athletes who identified as male and members of university-sponsored varsity athletic teams; were over age 18 years, and endorsed body dissatisfaction (i.e., scores greater than 1 on the overweight preoccupation or appearance orientation subscales of the multidimensional body self relations questionnaire, or scores greater than 5 on the appearance orientation subscales)
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perceptual dimension of body image and self-esteem
Related_Factor_sub-class 3: Judgement of size, shape and weight
Authors' conclusions: This studies clarifies notable correlates, particularly overweight preoccupation, of eating pathology in male athletes and highlights sport confidence as a potential prevention and intervention target.
Limits: Causality cannot be inffered from cross sectional findings and the causality of risk factors for eating pathology in male athletes remains unclear. Internal consistency of the purging subscale of the EPSI was poor. Alternately, the items composing this subscale may not adequately reflect compensatory purging behaviors or its underlying motivations in this population.
Perspectives: Future research would benefit from a larger sample without preset body dissatisfaction criteria to ensure adequate power for moderation, to allow for direct comparison across sport types, positions, and competition levels, and to avoid potential floor effects. More longitudinal and mediational designs are needed to model how sport related pressures relate to these varied correlates.

Authors' conclusions: Peer and romantic pressure collectively predicted Females body image, disordered eating behaviors, and self esteem, romantic pressure did not significantly contribute independently. Peer pressure positively predicted disordered eating behaviors.

Perspectives: It is important to promote resistance to sociocultural pressures (parents, peers, media) and pressures from coaches in disordered eating prevention programmes for female athletes of all ages participating in sports irrespective of sport group WS or less. Choaches must be educated to understand and recognise the associations between athletes body image, disordered eating, and physical, mental health and sports performance, as weel as their personal influence on it and to promote positive body image in sports environments.

19 athletes with eating disorders
33 without disordered eating
Inclusion criteria: High performance Female athletes with disordered eating ; competing on national or international levels ; control without disordered eating. Subjects with disordered eating meet two of the major criteria: amaleorrhoea, low BMI or low body fat, purging methods, and bulimic episodes, in addition to two of the following minor criteria: fear of weight gain, feelings of fatness, maintained low weight and increased importance of weight/shape. If participants did not meet these criteria, they were placed in the control group without disordered eating.
Mean_BMI:
Athletes with disordered eating M=20.69, SD=2.89
Athletes without disordered eating M=20.23, SD=2.23
Mean_Years of experience:
Athletes with disordered eating M=9, SD=4.27
Athletes without disordered eating M=8.36, SD=4.09
Related_Factor_measure: Contextual Body Image Questionnaire for Athletes (CBIQA)
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perceptual dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: The athletic body image strongly contributed to ED. The athletes self-evaluations about shape, weight and fat percentage and the perceived opinions of others on these aspects appeared to be only significant factors uniquely explaining 14 and 9% of the EDE-Q variance. 64% of the variance was explained by the relevant body image components from daily life and sport.
Limits: Limitations of the present study were its sample size and consitution. Unfortunately, the number of Dutch high performance athletes is not that extensive.
Perspectives: Future studies should further explore athletes body comparisons in daliy life and sport, and possible differences between athletes with and without disordered eating in this respect. Future research should further explore body images in sport and daily life, particularly in athletes with disordered eating. We needed to extent the sample with a group of at-risk athletes who were not professionaly diagnosed in advance. Future investigation needs to take into account dynamic and contextual body image changes. It should also focus more closely on why certain athletes develop a more negative body image and how this could be prevented.

Title: Psychosocial correlates of disordered eating among male collegiate athletes
Authors: Petrie, T.A., Greenleaf, C., Carter, J.E., & Reel, J.J.
Population subgroup:
Asymptomatic group based on their QEDD responses (n=164)
Symptomatic group based on their QEDD responses (n=35)
Inclusion criteria: Male collegiate athletes from three different NCAA division I institutions located in the Midwest, Southwest and Mountain regions of the US
Mean_Years of experience:
College level M=1.81, SD=1.30
M=8.70, SD=5.28
Related_Factor_measure: How afraid are you becoming fat ?
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perceptual dimension of body image and self-esteem
Related_Factor_sub-class 3: Judgement of size, shape and weight
Authors' conclusions: The psychosocial factors generally were unrelated to level of eating pathology. The male athletes were healthy in terms of their eating behaviors, had few negative mood concerns, were moderately satisfied with their bodies and experienced few pressures from personal and societal sources to change their weight or body size/shape.
Limits: Negative mood was represented by a single-item measures, this may have affected the relationship with disordered eating. All data are based on athlete self report and thus are subject to mono-method bias as well as underreporting that might occur when assessing sensitive areas. Only two of the male athletes were classified as having an eating disorder and both had an ED-NOS.
Perspectives: Researchers should use measures of specific mood states (e.g., depression, anxiety) that are based on multiple items (e.g., PANAS-X), include measures of positive mood state (e.g., optimism, happiness, confidence) and incorporate designs (e.g., longitudinal) that allow these questions to be addressed directly. Professionals should be attuned to looking for subclinical level presentations of symptoms among the athletes with whom they work. Professionals may want to work proactively with male athletic teams, educating them about healthy, nutritional eating and maintaing regular exercise during the off-season. Such approaches may assist male collegiate athletes during the shift from the structural regimen that occurs when in-season and the potentially more relaxed, self-initiated approach that is taken during the off season.

Authors' conclusions: The psychosocial factors generally were unrelated to level of eating pathology. Title: Overweight preoccupation is associated with eating pathology in male collegiate athletes with body dissatisfaction
Authors: Murray, M.F., Perelman, H., Sandhu, D., Quinones, I.C., & Haedt-Matt, A.A.
Inclusion criteria: Collegiate athletes who identified as male and members of university-sponsored varsity athletic teams; were over age 18 years, and endorsed body dissatisfaction (i.e., scores greater than 1 on the overweight preoccupation or appearance orientation subscales of the multidimensional body self relations questionnaire, or scores greater than 5 on the appearance orientation subscales)
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perceptual dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: This studies clarifies notable correlates, particularly overweight preoccupation, of eating pathology in male athletes and highlights sport confidence as a potential prevention and intervention target.
Limits: Causality cannot be inffered from cross sectional findings and the causality of risk factors for eating pathology in male athletes remains unclear. Internal consistency of the purging subscale of the EPSI was poor. Alternately, the items composing this subscale may not adequately reflect compensatory purging behaviors or its underlying motivations in this population.
Perspectives: Future research would benefit from a larger sample without preset body dissatisfaction criteria to ensure adequate power for moderation, to allow for direct comparison across sport types, positions, and competition levels, and to avoid potential floor effects. More longitudinal and mediational designs are needed to model how sport related pressures relate to these varied correlates.

Title: Contextual body image and athletes' disordered eating: the contribution of athletic body image to disordered eating in high performance Female athletes
Authors: Karin de Bruin, A.P., Oudejans, R.R.D., Bakker, F.C., & Woertman, L.
Population subgroup:
19 athletes with eating disorders
33 without disordered eating
Inclusion criteria: High performance Female athletes with disordered eating ; competing on national or international levels ; control without disordered eating. Subjects with disordered eating meet two of the major criteria: amaleorrhoea, low BMI or low body fat, purging methods, and bulimic episodes, in addition to two of the following minor criteria: fear of weight gain, feelings of fatness, maintained low weight and increased importance of weight/shape. If participants did not meet these criteria, they were placed in the control group without disordered eating.
Mean_BMI:
Athletes with disordered eating M=20.69, SD=2.89
Athletes without disordered eating M=20.23, SD=2.23
Mean_Years of experience:
Athletes with disordered eating M=9, SD=4.27
Athletes without disordered eating M=8.36, SD=4.09
Related_Factor_measure: Contextual Body Image Questionnaire for Athletes (CBIQA)
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perceptual dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: The athletic body image strongly contributed to ED. The athletes self-evaluations about shape, weight and fat percentage and the perceived opinions of others on these aspects appeared to be only significant factors uniquely explaining 14 and 9% of the EDE-Q variance. 64% of the variance was explained by the relevant body image components from daily life and sport.
Limits: Limitations of the present study were its sample size and consitution. Unfortunately, the number of Dutch high performance athletes is not that extensive.
Perspectives: Future studies should further explore athletes body comparisons in daliy life and sport, and possible differences between athletes with and without disordered eating in this respect. Future research should further explore body images in sport and daily life, particularly in athletes with disordered eating. We needed to extent the sample with a group of at-risk athletes who were not professionaly diagnosed in advance. Future investigation needs to take into account dynamic and contextual body image changes. It should also focus more closely on why certain athletes develop a more negative body image and how this could be prevented.

Title: Psychosocial correlates of disordered eating among male collegiate athletes
Authors: Petrie, T.A., Greenleaf, C., Carter, J.E., & Reel, J.J.
Population subgroup:
Asymptomatic group based on their QEDD responses (n=164)
Symptomatic group based on their QEDD responses (n=35)
Inclusion criteria: Male collegiate athletes from three different NCAA division I institutions located in the Midwest, Southwest and Mountain regions of the US
Mean_Years of experience:
College level M=1.81, SD=1.30
M=8.70, SD=5.28
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perceptual dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: The psychosocial factors generally were unrelated to level of eating pathology. The male athletes were healthy in terms of their eating behaviors, had few negative mood concerns, were moderately satisfied with their bodies and experienced few pressures from personal and societal sources to change their weight or body size/shape.
Limits: Negative mood was represented by a single-item measures, this may have affected the relationship with disordered eating. All data are based on athlete self report and thus are subject to mono-method bias as well as underreporting that might occur when assessing sensitive areas. Only two of the male athletes were classified as having an eating disorder and both had an ED-NOS.
Perspectives: Researchers should use measures of specific mood states (e.g., depression, anxiety) that are based on multiple items (e.g., PANAS-X), include measures of positive mood state (e.g., optimism, happiness, confidence) and incorporate designs (e.g., longitudinal) that allow these questions to be addressed directly. Professionals should be attuned to looking for subclinical level presentations of symptoms among the athletes with whom they work. Professionals may want to work proactively with male athletic teams, educating them about healthy, nutritional eating and maintaing regular exercise during the off-season. Such approaches may assist male collegiate athletes during the shift from the structural regimen that occurs when in-season and the potentially more relaxed, self-initiated approach that is taken during the off season.

Title: The relationship between perceived stress, body image and eating behaviors in athletes
Authors: Şentürk, G., Deliceoğlu, G., Atasoy, M., & Yıldırım, İ.G.
Journal: Research in Sport Education and Sciences
Inclusion criteria: Athletes between the ages of 13-23 who volunteered to participate
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perceptual dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: Perfectionism in athletes is linked to higher stress, eating disturbances, and body perception issues, with women showing higher stress, emotional eating, and restrictive eating behaviors. Emotional states significantly influence eating patterns, highlighting the need for psychological and nutritional support in sports contexts
Limits: Findings are partly inconsistent with previous studies (e.g., gender differences), and results may depend on specific sports or samples. The study also relies on self-reported measures, which may introduce bias
Perspectives: Future research should further explore emotional eating across different sports and genders, and develop targeted interventions. Integrating psychological support, education, and nutritional guidance could help improve athletes’ well-being and performance
Sport_name_original: Taekwondo, rowing

Title: Psychometric properties of the contextual body image questionnaire for athletes: a replication and extension study in Female collegiate athletes
Authors: Stewart, T., Kilpela, L., Wesley, K., & Becker, C.
Inclusion criteria: Female athletes at each university within the ages of 17-27 years
Related_Factor_measure: Contextual Body Image Questionnaire for Athletes (CBIQA)
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perceptual dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: Daily life thin-fat others correlated with EDE-Q global scores. Sport muscularity did not correlated with EDE-Q. All dimensions except muscularity correlated with all subscales in both contexts. Appearance dimension (perceiving others opinions of yourself) was related to higher levels of ED pathology in both daily life and sport contexts. Self evaluation and perceived other evaluation as fatter were also related to more ED pathology. Muscularity in daily life was not related to ED symptomatology. CBIQA scores related to appearance may predict future ED pathology.
Limits: Reliance on self-report data, attrition at follow-up, and that the CBIQA was delivered to participants 12 months into the FAB program as opposed to the beginning of the parent trial.
Perspectives: Further research on cntextual body images is needed to evaluate the impact of these dual body images with Female athletes not only while in sport, but while away or retiring from sport, inclusding periods of injury, between seasons and when completing sport.

Inclusion criteria: Female figure skaters aged 12 to 25. Former skaters, basic skills skaters, and those in adult skating programs (e.g., age-based competitions following adult test equivalencies) were excluded
Related_Factor: Self consciousness of weight and appearance
Related_Factor_measure: Sport Related Weight Pressures in Sport Scale-Females (WPS-F)
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perceptual dimension of body image and self-esteem
Related_Factor_sub-class 4: Self consciousness of weight and appearance
Authors' conclusions: All sport related weight pressures were significantly related to disordered eating, however only self consciousness of weight and appearance emerged as a significant correlate in the regression model. Body dissatisfaction explained an additional 5.7% of the variance in disordered eating. Sport related body dissatisfaction also emerged as a significant predictor. Positive perfectionism made a significant contribution, but negative perfectionism did not. Self esteem may not be strongly related to disordered eating. Athletic identity did not emerge as a significant variable in the final regression model, although the bivariate correlation indicated a significant positive relationship with disordered eating.
Limits: Societal weight pressures were not exmained. Self report nature of the surveys and the willingness of athletes to honestly and accurately respond to survey items. The results are also based on a conveniance sample of skaters limited to clubs in the Midwest and Northeast. Cross sectional design, causal relationships and change over time could not be determined.
Perspectives:
Sport psychology practiitioners should aid this effort by teaching skaters to appreciate body strengths and utilize psychological skills that may buffer the impact of negative weight pressures (e.g., utilizing positive self talk and realistic goal-setting). 
A random and more representative sample of skaters nationally and internationally, inclusive of males, should be considered in future research.

Title: Structural equation modeling of risk factors for the development of eating disorder symptoms in Female athleres
Authors: Williamson, D.A., Netemeyer, R.G., Jackman, L.P., Anderson, D.A., Funsch, C.L., Rabalais, J.Y.
Inclusion criteria: Female college athletes from a major state university
DEAB_measure: Interview for Diagnoses of Eating Disorders (IDED)
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perceptual dimension of body image and self-esteem
Related_Factor_sub-class 3: Judgement of size, shape and weight
Authors' conclusions: Overconcern with body size was a primary and strong mediator of other risk factors for developing eating disorder symptoms. Risk factors that were mediated by overconcern with body size were: social influence for thinness, anxiety about athletic performance, and negative appraisal of athletic achievement. These risk factors were not strongly predictive of eating disorder symptoms without mediation through overconcern with body size.

Title: The contribution of BMI, body image inflexibility, and generalized anxiety to symptoms of eating disorders and exercise dependence in exercisers
Authors: Zou, L., Yang, P., Herold, F., Liu,  W., Szabo, A., Taylor, A., Sun, J., & Ji, L.
Journal: International Journal of mental Health Promotion
Inclusion criteria: University students; habitual exercisers; exercise frequency 3 times per week
Mean_BMI:
Male M=22.12, SD=2.38
Female M=20.55, SD=2.21
Sport M=21.53, SD=2.14
Non sport M=21.29, SD=3.10
Related_Factor_measure: Body Image Acceptance and Action Questionnaire (BI-AAQ)
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perceptual dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: BMI and body image inflexibility are predictive of eating disorders symptoms.
Limits: All measures rely on self reports, they are somewhat prone to measurement error that arises from self report bias. BMI has some disadvantages; BMI is biased because this measure does not take into account the difference between muscle mass and fat mass. The participants comprise only universities students. This study focuses on body image distorsion as one of the predictors while other possible variables such as self compassion, perfectionism, and obsessive compulsive personality disorder were not considered. The cross sectional design does not allow the examination of causality and the direction of the pathways.
Perspectives: Our findings suggest that the prevention and treatment of exercise dependence symptoms should consider interventions to improve the indivdiuals attitude towards the perception of their own body by addressing body image inflexibility.

Title: Perfectionism, body satisfaction and dieting in athletes: the role of gender and sport type
Authors: Prnjak, K., Jukic, I., & Tufano, J.J.
Inclusion criteria: Athletes aged from 18 to 29 years from the faculty of Kinesiology
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Authors' conclusions: Perfectionism and body satisfaction explain dieting among Female athletes. For the male athletes, none of the predictors contributed to the understanding of their dieting behaviour. In addition, age, sport type and duration of sport participation did not contribute to dieting behaviour un case of male and Female. Adaptive and maladaptive perfectionism were associated with body satisfaction among Female athletes but not with dieting behaviour directly. Satisfaction with one's body was shown to be the largest independent predictor of dieting and their relationship was negative.
Limits: The data was based on self reported measures. Cross sectional design limits the causal inference between perfectionism, body satisfaction and dieting. The sample consisted of athletes who were enrolled in a university program which might limit the generalizability. PANPS should not be used as a measure of perfectionism due to a questionable factor validity of the positive perfectionism subscale. EAT-26 was shown to have a low positive predictive value due to the rarity of targeted conditions while two out of three EAT-26 subscales demonstrated low internal consistency and omitting them while investigating eating disorder may not be the best approach. The number of Female participants was lower than males, which might have affected some of the analysis were gender-split was included.
Perspectives: It would be important to further etablish the relationship between perfectionism dimensions and body satisfaction in the area of disordered eating but also take a consideration the context in which athletes perceive their body.
Sport_name_original: Soccer; basketball; gymnastics; figure skating; athletics; swimming

40 Athletes competing in rhythmic gymnastics
40 Athletes competing in football
40 Non-athletes
Inclusion criteria: Membership in Spanish sport clubs or rhythmic gymnastics, or footballers with a background > 4 years of systematic training and competitive experience, training a minimum of 8h per week, with absence of severe injuries
Mean_Age:
Gymnasts M=16.6, SD=2.62
Footballers M=17.98, SD=3.42
Mean_BMI:
M=20.63, SD=2.77
Gymnasts M=18.72, SD=1.54
Footballers M=22.45, SD=2.93
Sporting population: Gymnasts group consisted of 5 elite competing internationally and 35 at the national level
Range_Exercise frequency:
Elites : 20-35h per week
National gymnasts : 12-20h per week
Footballers : 4 training sessions plus a competitive match per week
Range_Years of experience: Minimum 4 years of training and competitive experience
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Authors' conclusions: Correlation obtained between anxiety (both trait and state) and the EAT-40 was positively and statistically significant. In the multiple regression analysis that was performed with SCOFF scores as a dependent variable, the most predictive variable was socially prescribed perfectionism. It showed negative correlation with EAT-40 and self esteem. Self esteem is probably a protective factor to develop an eating disorder despite perfectionism, which is the most predictive variable as the multiple linear regression showed, and this variable was high in athletes.
Limits: Small sample size. No precise clinical diagnostic data were available to validate ED screening in the current study.
Perspectives:
In the future, the use of other kinds of measurements, less subjected to the desirability bias, would help to discriminate whether the improvements in self-esteem and eating disorders in elite gymnasts are due to this bias or to preventing psychological treatments and trainings by coaches.
 In addition, it is important to further explore the impact of other psychological factors on eating disordered behaviours such as body image, mood, depression or motivation, among others; due to the fact that they imply multifactorial aetiology of disorders.

Title: Frequency and psychosocial correlates of eating disorder symptomatology in male figure skaters
Authors: Voelker, D.K., Petrie, T.A., Reel, J.J., & Gould, D.
Inclusion criteria: Male figure skaters
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Authors' conclusions: Negative perfectionism, self esteem, and athletic identity were unrelated to ED symptomatology.
Limits: Smaller sample. Weight pressures may be experienced differently according to discipline specific performance demands. Cross sectional design.
Perspectives:
Future research should incorporate longitudinal designs to identify true risk factors of ED symptomatology and use qualitative interviews to further examine the lived experience of sport-related weight pressures. 
Practitioners may collaborate with other professionals, such as sports dieteticians, to educate skating communities on weight-performance myths and improve communication between skaters, parents, and coaches about the body. Practitioners may also assist athletes in coping with weight pressures by focusing on body appreciation and function while reinforcing that healthy training approaches can have positive effects on eating, exercise, and body image.

Title: Relationships between personality traits and disordered eating among Chinese Female exercisers: the role of symptoms of exercise dependence and obsessive-compulsiveness
Authors: Yang, P., Wang, T., Herold, F., Muller, N.G., Taylor, A., Szabo, A., Granziol, U., Cook, B., Landolfi, E., Somi, M., & Zou, L.
Inclusion criteria: The Female exercises needed to be training at least three times per week for a minimum of 150 min in total, for not less than six months with respect to the recruitmalet date.
Mean_Exercise frequency:
M=4.42 times a week, SD=1.88
74.14min every session
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Related_Factor_sub-class 3: Adaptive personality traits for the UEAB studies available to date
Authors' conclusions: Only the personality traits conscientiousness, emotional stability and agreeableness are significantly associated with disordered eating. Our mediation analyses revealed the relationship between conscientiousness and disordered eating was completely mediated via the path of exercise dependence and obsessive compulsive symptoms, while the relationship of emotional stability and disordered eating was partly mediated via exercise dependence symptoms and obsessive compulsive symptoms. Moreover the relationship between agreeableness and disordered eating was only mediated by the severity of obsessive compulsive symptoms. The results of the correaltion analysis revealed that conscientiousness, emotional stability and agreeableness were negatively associated with the severity of disordered eating. In contrast, extroversion and openness to experience did not show a significant association with ED. The multiple mediation model of conscientiousness on disordered eating revaled an indirect effect of conscientiousness on disordered eating via higher exercise dependence symptoms and higher obsessive compulsive symptoms. The multiple mediation model of the effects of emotiona stability on disordered eating demonstrated an indirect effect of emotional stability via exercise dependence and obsessive compulsive symptoms. Considering the single mediation model of agreeableness on disordered eating, our results showed that the relationship between agreeableness and disordered eating can be explained through obsessive compulsive symptoms.
Limits: This cross sectional study design did not allow conclusions concerning the causal relationship. Symptoms of disordered eating were considered but we did not distinguish between different types of eating disorders, which may limit the generalizabiliy. Only Chinese Female exercisers were included. The inclusion of personality traits was operationalized by using the well etablished big five personality model. However, given that personality traits (e.g., perfectionism) were also identified as core characteristics among these disorders
Perspectives: Other personality dimensions or mechanisms should be examined in future studies to allow for more robust and nuanced conclusions.

Title: Index of healthy eating and emotional eating in relation to psychological inflexibility in dance students
Authors: Arbinaga, F., Mendoza-Sierra, M.I., Fernandez-Acosta, G.
Inclusion criteria: To be of legal age, to have been studying dance for at least 3 years and always with a teacher, to be enrolled in a conservatory course (elementary, intermediate, or professional level) or dance school-academy
Mean_Exercise frequency:
4.72 (1.22) days per week
20.31 (11.73) hours per week
DEAB_measure: The Eating and Appraisal Due to Emotions and Stress Questionnaire (EADES)
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Related_Factor_sub-class 3: Adaptive personality traits for the UEAB studies available to date
Authors' conclusions: Students with high psychological inflexibility reported greater use of food as an emotion regulator.
Limits: The design used does not allow for establishing causal relationships that determine the directionality between the variables analyzed. It could be worthwhile to use a larger sample and control more rigorously the variables related to dance.
Perspectives: It would be interesting to analyze whether the index of healthy eating and emotional eating is related in a different way to psychological inflexibility according to the specialty of dance. It would be interesting to analyze the impact of psychological inflexibility across a ranges of specialities, considering the importance of weight in each dance discipline. Dance education can be understood from a perspective that considers the dancer-teacher dyad.

Title: Athletic identity and disordered eating in obligatory and non-obligatory runners
Authors: Gapin, J.I., & Petruzzello, S.J.
Inclusion criteria: Participants were recruited from running clubs, road races, and kinesiology classes at a large Midwestern university. The only inclusion criterion was that participant be over the age of 18.
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Authors' conclusions: There is relationships among obligatory exercise and DE. Athletic identity had a significant positive correlation with disordered eating attitudes and behaviours. Athletic identity correlated with both drive for thinness and perfectionism. The negative affectivity correlated with all the disordered eating measures. The hypothesis that athletic identity would mediate the effect of obligatory running on disordered eating was not supported.
Limits: All measures were self-report in nature. Not all the subscales of the Eating Disorder Inventory have been validated in athletic samples and there is some concern that the Eating disorder Inventory may not be accurate in identiying those athletes at risk for an eating disorder.
Perspectives: Obligatory and non obligatory runners were dichotomized. It is likely, however, that this form of exercise occurs on a continuum and it would be valuable to assess this. Longitudinal research of those at risk form becoming obligatory runners could determine whether th shift towards obligatory running patterns occurs immediately after adopting an exercise regimen or whether the change occurs over time as they progress in training frequency, duration, and intensity. Further research using the Athletic Identity Measurement Scale in a variety of athletic population is necessary. Future studies should examine other mediating variables related to identity (motivation to exercise are variables associated with DE and obligatory exercise). When examining obligatory runners it may be helpful to look at Deci and Ryan's (1985, 2000) self-determination theory as an explanation for obligatory exercisers motivations to engage in exercise. It would be helpful to use the regulation in exercise questionnaire in conjunction with the obligatory exercise questionnaire and eating disorder measures to evaluate in more detail why certain individuals are more susceptible to unhealthy exercise attitudes and behaviours than others.

Title: Understanding athletic and exercise identity in relation to disordered eating behaviors
Authors: Palermo, M., & Rancourt, D.
Inclusion criteria: Undergraduate students self identifying as athletes
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Authors' conclusions:
Study 1 : athletic identity was not associated with global disordered eating behaviors. 
Study 2 : athletic identity appeared to be associated with less cognitive restraint and was not significantly associated with other measures of disordered eating. Only exercise identity was associated with disordered eating.
Limits: Different disordered eating measures were used across study 1 and 2. Neither study 1 nor study 2 collected data about level of sport participation. Both studies were cross-sectional. This study included a broad sample of university students and findings may not generalize to other populations.
Perspectives: Exercise identity may be an important risk factor to consider in future research related to disordered eating and exercise behaviors in college students.

Title: Athlete identity and eating pathology in distance runners: when compulsive exercise matters
Authors: Gorrell, S., & Anderson, D.A.
Inclusion criteria: Adult distance runners; registered for either a full or half marathon in the upstate region of New York
Mean_BMI:
Male M=24.11, SD=3.07
Female M=22.63, SD=2.81
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Authors' conclusions: Regression analyses indicated that increased identity with exercise contributed to decreased eating pathology amongst half marathon runners. There was a significant interaction effect noted between exercise identity and compulsive exercise, such that the relation of exercise identity and eating disorders pathology was significant amongst those runners reporting either lower or higher compulsive exercise scores. The significant associations identified for half marathoners were not demonstrated in marathon runners.
Limits: It is possible that individuals registered for the half marathon were of a more elite running status. This study was also dependent on cross-sectional, self reported data collection methods. The runners assessed were all adults who were registered for competitive events in the northeastern United States, and results may not necessarily generalize to other age groups, or geographical areas, including internationally.
Perspectives:
Future work should investigate the relation between the study variables over time, allowing for investigation of the impact of athlete injury. Investigate variables amongst runners who are adolescent and young adult. 
Clinicians should increase screening for eating disorders and compulsive exercise across runners of less elite status, and integrate eating disorders prevention efforts amongst athletes who report low exercise identity and either lower or higher compulsive exercise.

Title: Understanding athletic and exercise identity in relation to disordered eating behaviors
Authors: Palermo, M., & Rancourt, D.
Inclusion criteria: Undergraduate students self identifying as athletes
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Authors' conclusions:
Study 1 : athletic identity was not associated with global disordered eating behaviors. 
Study 2 : athletic identity appeared to be associated with less cognitive restraint and was not significantly associated with other measures of disordered eating. Only exercise identity was associated with disordered eating.
Limits: Different disordered eating measures were used across study 1 and 2. Neither study 1 nor study 2 collected data about level of sport participation. Both studies were cross-sectional. This study included a broad sample of university students and findings may not generalize to other populations.
Perspectives: Exercise identity may be an important risk factor to consider in future research related to disordered eating and exercise behaviors in college students.

Title: Body Talk, Athletic Identity, and Eating Disorder Symptoms in male
Authors: Ahlich, E., Choquette, E.M., Rancourt, D.
Inclusion criteria: 18-35 years; recruited using convenience sampling from a large southeastern university's research; receiving research credit upon completion of the study; informed consent
Related_Factor_measure: Single item asking participants if they considered themselves to be an athlete
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Authors' conclusions: The current findings support body talk and fat talk as a potential risk factor for eating disorders among male. Muscle-focused body talk may not a risk factor for diagnostic eating disorder symptoms. Muscle talk among male is related less to muscle dissatisfaction and more to male socioalization processes. Athletic identity did non emerge as a significant moderator of the association between body talk and eating disorder symptoms.
Limits: The study was limited to a single university campus in the southeastern United States, limiting generalizability of the findings. Few participants endorsed aesthetic or lean sports, potentially attenuating results.
Perspectives:
Future work may benefit from using a more objective of body composition. 
Future work should explore such associations among male in a clinical sample, examining whether fat or muscle talk is associated with eating disorder and/or muscle dysmorphia symptom severity. 
Fat talk may be an important prevention target amon male, regardless of athletic identity.

Title: Prevalence of orthorexia nervosa and association with mental health among Palestinian physical education students - cross sectional study
Authors: Al-Amouri, F.M., Abualhaija, R., Al Atrash, M., Abu Alwafa, R., AlTamimi, M., Badrasawi, M.
Journal: BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation
Inclusion criteria: Students from the physical education department at An-Najah National University
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Authors' conclusions: This study highlights a higher risk of orthorexia nervosa (OrNe) among male students, with strong associations with dieting behaviors and, in females, BMI. It emphasizes the multifactorial nature of OrNe and the importance of early identification in young athletes.
Limits: The cross-sectional design limits causal inference, and self-reported measures may introduce bias. Additionally, mental health assessment tools and limited comparability with prior studies restrict interpretation.
Perspectives: Future research should include longitudinal designs, more diverse populations, and more specific mental health measures. Preventive strategies targeting dietary behaviors and body-related factors in university and sports settings are needed.

Title: Influence of perfectionism on variables associated to eating disorders in dance students
Authors: Arcelus, J., Garcia-Dantas, A., Sanchez-Martin, M., Del Rio, C.
Inclusion criteria: Female dance professionals; aged 12-20;  from two professional dance conservatories in Spain; informed consent was obtained from their parents.
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Authors' conclusions: Body image has been found, not only to be a risk factor for the development of an ED, but as a mediator between perfectionism and dieting, and associated to performance cognitive anxiety which mediates the relationship between perfectionism and depression.
Limits: The use of general questionnaires such as the BDI II or EAT-26 which are not validated specifically to be used within the dance population, although they are validated and highly reliable measurements. Performance anxiety was measured hypothetically and it will be best to measure it previous to an event. Performance anxiety has been retrospectively measured instead of administering the questionnaires in situ before the performance.
Perspectives: Interventions aiming at reducing concern over mistakes may required a preventative component and by doing so it will help reducing body dissatisfaction, performance cognitive anxiety and dieting which will prevent the development of eating disorders in this vulnerable group. Future research should replicate this study and include males different age range, dance levels and nationalities.

Inclusion criteria: Female; aged 12-20; participation was voluntary; informed consent was obtained from their parents.
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Authors' conclusions: Body image has been found, not only to be a risk factor for the development of an ED, but as a mediator between perfectionism and dieting, and associated to performance cognitive anxiety which mediates the relationship between perfectionism and depression.
Limits: The use of general questionnaires such as the BDI II or EAT-26 which are not validated specifically to be used within the dance population, although they are validated and highly reliable measurements. Performance anxiety was measured hypothetically and it will be best to measure it previous to an event. Performance anxiety has been retrospectively measured instead of administering the questionnaires in situ before the performance.
Perspectives: Interventions aiming at reducing concern over mistakes may required a preventative component and by doing so it will help reducing body dissatisfaction, performance cognitive anxiety and dieting which will prevent the development of eating disorders in this vulnerable group. Future research should replicate this study and include males different age range, dance levels and nationalities.

Title: Eating attitudes, body appreciation, perfectionism, and the risk of exercise addiction in physically active adults: a cluster analysis
Authors: Piko, B.F., Berki, T.L., Kun, O., Mellor, D.
Inclusion criteria: 18 years of age and have an active lifestyle with regular physical activity (at least once a week, for a minimum of 30min)
Mean_Exercise frequency: 1h or less/week n=72 1-2h/week n=114 3-5h/week n=16 >5h/week n=3
Mean_Years of experience: 1 year or less n=40 2-3 years n=24 3-5 years n=17 5-10 years n=37 >10 years n=87
DEAB_measure: Validated Hungarian version of the Eating Attitude Test-26 (EAT-26)
Related_Factor: Concern over mistakes and doubts about actions
Related_Factor_measure: Hungarian version of the Frost Multidimensional Perfectionism Scale (FMPS)
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Authors' conclusions: Exercise addiction (EA) can also occur in regular exercisers, not just athletes, and is often linked with disordered eating (DE) when body image concerns and perfectionism are present. These factors interact in complex ways, meaning EA is not always pathological but can signal risk when combined with unhealthy eating attitudes and excessive performance pressure
Limits: The cross-sectional design prevents causal conclusions, and reliance on self-reports, a relatively small and female-biased sample, and heterogeneous sport types limit generalizability
Perspectives: Future research should use larger, more diverse samples and longitudinal designs, while exploring additional psychological variables and protective factors to better understand and prevent EA and DE

Title: The Body shape of pubertal rhythmic gymnasts: the association with BMI, eating disorder risks, and perfectionism
Authors: Marković, A., Veljković, A.A., Jurišić, M.V., Obradović, A., Đurović, D.
Inclusion criteria: Female rhythmic gymnasts, affiliated with different rhythmic gymnastics clubs in the Balkans
Sporting population: National level tournaments and international cups
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Authors' conclusions: Body shape concerns in pubertal rhythmic gymnasts are associated with disordered eating attitudes and maladaptive perfectionism, increasing vulnerability to eating disorders.
Limits: The study is limited by a small, specific sample, self-reported data, and a cross-sectional design without a control group. These factors restrict generalizability and prevent causal conclusions
Perspectives: Future research should include larger and more diverse samples and use longitudinal designs, especially during puberty. Early interventions targeting body image and perfectionism could help reduce eating disorder risk

Title: Perfectionism and eating psychopathology among dancers: the role of high standards and self-criticism
Authors: Goodwin, H., Arcelus, J., Geach, N., & Meyer, C.
Inclusion criteria: Female; aged 18 years or older; current member of a university recreational dance club; clubs comprised ballet, modern, tap, jazz, and/or hi hop disciplines. The participants were not screened for previous or current eating disorder treatment.
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Authors' conclusions: High standards and self criticism are positively associated with eating restraint, eating concern, weight concern and shape concern. The associations between self-criticism and eating pathology were not moderated by high standards. Self criticism fully mediated the relationships between high standards and restraint, eating concern, weight concern and shape concern.
Limits: The self report nature of the data means reports may be unreliable and subject to social desirability bias. The method of participants recruitlent precluded any analysis of response rate, and it was not known whether or not there was a bias to those who chose to participate versus those who did not participate. The heterogeneous nature of the sample means that underlying group differences (between dance style, competency level and hours of dance practice) may have been missed.
Perspectives: The relationships between high standards, self-criticism and eating disorder risk requires examination in more homogenous sub-groups of dancers, to further identify the risk environments for eating psychopathology.

Title: Perfectionism and eating attitudes in competitive rowers: moderating effects of body mass, weight classification and gender
Authors: Haase, A.M., Prapavessis, H., & Owens, G.
Inclusion criteria: National level heavyweight and lightweight rowers from New Zealand and Australia
Mean_Age:
Female M=20.08, SD=4.23
Male M=21.49, SD=4.67
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Authors' conclusions: After controlling for social desirability effects, negative perfectionism scores were found to correlate positively with disturbed eating attitudes scores, whereas positive perfectionism scores were found to be unrelated to disturbed eating attitude scores.
Limits: Focus only on rowing sample.
Perspectives:
This would suggest that resiliency against unhealthy eating could be increased by teaching athletes how to develop and maintain high levels of positive perfectionism. Intervention with goal in mind is a worthy topic for future research. 
Do these perfectionistic tendencies change throughout an athlete's career ? How and why do these changes occur ? What implications do these changes have on eating attitude ?
Sport_name_original: Rowing (i.e., Heavyweight and lightweight rowing)

Title: Impact of perfectionism on the risk of the female athlete triad in collegiate athletes
Authors: Brooks, S.G., Peach, H.D., Howden, R., Lowrie, J., Marino, J.S.
Journal: The Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
Inclusion criteria: NCAA female student-athletes between the ages of 18 and 24 years at a Division I university
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Authors' conclusions: This study found significant correlations between LEA risk, DE, triad risk, perfectionism and time spent in a program for female NCAA division I athletes
Limits: Sample size of the study. The athletes came from the same institutions. Study did not collect detailed dietary information, such as macronutrient composition, we did use validated methods of interpreting athletes eating attitudes and behaviors. No causal relationship between perfectionism and our outcomes could be established because this was a cross-sectional study.
Perspectives: Future research should investigate possible interventions to hemp athletes manifest their perfectionistic tendencies in adaptive dimensions rather than maladaptive dimensions associated with an increased risk. Other psychological variables (drive for thinness, self esteem) should also benefit explored to further our understanding of the role of mental health in athletes risk for adverse health conditions.
Sport_name_original: Cross country, soccer, softball, tennis, track throws, track sprints

Title: Compulsive exercise as a mediator between clinical perfectionism and eating pathology
Authors: Egan, S.J., Bodill, K., Watson, H.J., Valentine, E., Shu, C., & Hagger, M.S.
Inclusion criteria: The population was adults over the age of 18 years who participated in a diverse range of sport and exercise. The inclusion criteria of exercice twice or more per week was chosen to include people who exercised regularly but the criterion was relatively low as amount of exercise in not the defiing feature of compulsive exercise.
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Authors' conclusions: Direct and indirect effects were found between clinical perfectionism and eating pathology through compulsive exercise. Specifically, there were direct effects of clinical perfectionism on avoidance/rule driven behavior, weight control exercise, and mood improvement.
Limits: Participant recruitmalet was not random or stratified which limits generalizability. The sample comprised mainly of individuals who are actively involved in one particular type of athletic poursuit: individual endurance sports and particularly running. The sample may, therefore, not be representative of individuals involved in sport and exercise in general. In addition, the study was cross-sectional, therefore the bidirectional relationship between eating pathology and compulsive exercise could not be assessed as this requires a longitudinal design. While we hypothesized that perfectionism would affect compulsive exercise, which would impact eating pathology, it could equally be argued that perfectionism influences eating pathology, which then influences compulsive exercise (i.e., compulsive exercise is a symptom of eating pathology, rather than an antecedent). Indeed, Meyer et al.’s (2011) model proposed bidirectional links between eating pathology and compulsive exercise. Meyer et al. (2011) argued that dieting and exercise reinforce one another due to social reinforcers which accompany the initial weight loss from regular exercise, which then intensifies eating, shape and weight concerns.
Perspectives: It would be useful to determine whether interventions for both perfectionism and compulsive exercise may help to improve the efficacy of standard treatments for eating disorders, above the gain already found in efficacious treatments such as CBT-E (Fairbunr et al., 2009) where clinical perfectionism is a focus if it is elevated. Future research could also examine the efficacy of specific stand-alone treatments for perfectionism (e.g., Egan et al., 2014) for compulsive exercise and perfectionism in eating disorders. Future research should measure perfectionism, compulsive exercise and eating pathology at two time points using a panel design and include a cross-lagged effects to determine the bidirectional relations between variables.

Title: Eating attitudes, body appreciation, perfectionism, and the risk of exercise addiction in physically active adults: a cluster analysis
Authors: Piko, B.F., Berki, T.L., Kun, O., Mellor, D.
Inclusion criteria: 18 years of age and have an active lifestyle with regular physical activity (at least once a week, for a minimum of 30min)
Mean_Exercise frequency: 1h or less/week n=72 1-2h/week n=114 3-5h/week n=16 >5h/week n=3
Mean_Years of experience: 1 year or less n=40 2-3 years n=24 3-5 years n=17 5-10 years n=37 >10 years n=87
DEAB_measure: The Hungarian validated version of the Exercise Addiction Inventory-Revised (EAI-R)
Related_Factor: Concern over mistakes and doubts about actions
Related_Factor_measure: Hungarian version of the Frost Multidimensional Perfectionism Scale (FMPS)
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Authors' conclusions: Exercise addiction (EA) can also occur in regular exercisers, not just athletes, and is often linked with disordered eating (DE) when body image concerns and perfectionism are present. These factors interact in complex ways, meaning EA is not always pathological but can signal risk when combined with unhealthy eating attitudes and excessive performance pressure
Limits: The cross-sectional design prevents causal conclusions, and reliance on self-reports, a relatively small and female-biased sample, and heterogeneous sport types limit generalizability
Perspectives: Future research should use larger, more diverse samples and longitudinal designs, while exploring additional psychological variables and protective factors to better understand and prevent EA and DE

Title: Perfectionism and learning experiences in dance class as risk factors for eating disorders in dancers
Authors: Penniment, K.J., & Egan, S.J.
Inclusion criteria: Being a Female aged between 18 and 30 years, currently studying classical and/or jazz ballet
Mean_BMI: 22.5% may be classified as underweight, with a BMI under 18.5kg/m²
Sporting population: 20.4% reported that they had danced semi professionally at one time, and 23.9% reported that they had danced at a professional level at one time.
Mean_Years of experience:
Dance tuition M=6.92, SD=22
Years studying dance M=14.5, SD=5.90
Related_Factor_CLASS: Intrapersonal factor related to unhealthy eating attitudes and behaviors
Authors' conclusions: The relation between perfectionism and eating disorders symptoms was partially mediated by thinness related learning. The hypothesis that the relationship between thinness related learning and eating disorders symptoms were partially mediated by thiness restricting expectancies was also supported. A direct relationship between perfectionism and eating disorders symptoms was found.
Limits: The data was cross sectional. Although the current model fit the data well, there are multiple other risk factors for ED and it is very likely that this risk is determined by multiple factors and is not simply a function of the emphasis on thinness in the dance environment, or perfectionism. The sample was too small to split into professional and non professional dancers to examine if the model was the same in these groups. Our view of perfectionism was aligned with the construct of clinical perfectionism, and as a result we examined a selected subset of scales from the FMPS and did not use relevant scales from the HMPS.
Perspectives:
It would be useful for future research to examine the efficacy of targeting young Female involved in dance with elevated levels of perfectionism for prevention programs, as preliminary findings are positive for the ability of programs targeting perfectionism to reduce eating disorders risk in Female adolescents. 
It would be useful for clinicians to consider directly targeting perfectionism through CBT programs for perfectionism in young Female involved in dance classes as it is likely to be a factor that puts them at higher risk of developing an eating disorders within this environment.
